sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Ji and fun

  • The ending ji tells the hour, and fun or pun tells the minutes. sanji is 3 o'clock, but sanpun is 3 minutes.
  • Say the hour first and the minutes after it: kuji juugofun is 9:15.
  • The word han means half past, so juuniji han is 12:30. You can also say the full minutes, sanjuppun.

Special o'clock readings

  • Only three hours are special: 4 o'clock is yoji, 7 o'clock is shichiji and 9 o'clock is kuji.
  • Do not say yonji, nanaji or kyuuji. They sound natural to a learner, but they are wrong.
  • The other hours are plain: ichiji, niji, sanji, goji, rokuji, hachiji, juuji, juuichiji and juuniji.

Fun or pun

  • pun goes with 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10: ippun, sanpun, yonpun, roppun, happun, juppun.
  • fun goes with 2, 5, 7 and 9: nifun, gofun, nanafun, kyuufun.
  • Bigger numbers follow the last digit: juugofun (15), nijuuippun (21), yonjuugofun (45).
  • Round tens take the squeezed sound: juppun (10), nijuppun (20), sanjuppun (30).

Gozen, gogo and han

  • gozen (a.m.) and gogo (p.m.) go in front of the time, never after it: gogo shichiji is 7 p.m.
  • han goes after the hour: gozen kuji han is 9:30 a.m.
  • gozen and gogo name a.m. and p.m. The words asa, hiru and yoru mean morning, noon and night.

Special months

  • April is shigatsu, July is shichigatsu and September is kugatsu.
  • Do not say yongatsu, nanagatsu or kyuugatsu.
  • The other months are plain: ichigatsu, nigatsu, sangatsu, gogatsu, rokugatsu, hachigatsu, juugatsu, juuichigatsu, juunigatsu.
  • The ending gatsu names a month on the calendar, like sangatsu (March). It does not count how many months pass.

Dates that are not number plus nichi

  • The 1st to the 10th are ten separate words: tsuitachi, futsuka, mikka, yokka, itsuka, muika, nanoka, youka, kokonoka, tooka.
  • Seven later dates are special: juuyokka (14th), juushichinichi (17th), juukunichi (19th), hatsuka (20th), nijuuyokka (24th), nijuushichinichi (27th), nijuukunichi (29th).
  • Every other date is the number plus nichi: juuichinichi (11th), juugonichi (15th), sanjuunichi (30th).

Dates that look alike

  • yokka is the 4th, and youka is the 8th. The 14th and 24th use yokka: juuyokka, nijuuyokka.
  • tooka is the 10th, and hatsuka is the 20th.
  • futsuka is the 2nd, and hatsuka is the 20th. Both end in ka, so check the start of the word.
  • muika is the 6th and nanoka is the 7th. Do not swap them.

Itsu, itsuka and itsutsu

  • The word itsu means when. itsuka is the 5th day of the month. itsutsu is five things.
  • ikutsu asks how many things, ikura asks a price, doko asks where, and itsu asks when.
  • If the answer is a date such as gogatsu itsuka (May 5), the question was nangatsu nannichi.

Years with 4 and 7

  • A year is the number plus nen, read like the big numbers from Chapter 3: sen kyuuhyaku kyuujuugonen is 1995.
  • When the last digit is 4, it becomes yo: nijuuyonen is the 24th year, so 2024 is nisen nijuuyonen.
  • When the last digit is 7, nana or shichi both work: juunananen and juushichinen.
  • The years in a full date go first: nisen juunananen ichigatsu kokonoka is January 9, 2017.

Big to small order

  • Dates go year, month, day. English often puts the year last, but Japanese puts it first.
  • Times go hour, then minutes: kuji juugofun.
  • A long time phrase goes from the biggest part to the smallest: raishuu no getsuyoubi gogo sanji.

Kara, made and choudo

  • The word kara means from, and made means until or up to. Each goes right after its own time.
  • gogo niji kara goji made is from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. Put kara after the first time and made after the second.
  • The word choudo means exactly. It goes before the time or after it: choudo sanji and sanji choudo are the same.

Goro or gurai

  • goro goes with a point in time: shichiji goro is around 7 o'clock.
  • gurai goes with an amount, such as a price (ikura gurai). You will use it for lengths of time in Chapter 5.
  • choudo says exactly and goro says around. Do not use both with the same time.

No or no no

  • Use no between a time word and a day or month: raishuu no getsuyoubi, kyonen no gogatsu.
  • Do not use no after mai: maishuu getsuyoubi is every Monday, not maishuu no getsuyoubi.
  • Use no between a day word and asa or yoru: kinou no asa, ashita no yoru.
  • kesa, konban, yuube, maiasa and maiban stand alone, so there is no no.

Last, this and next

  • For weeks and months, sen is last, kon is this, rai is next and sara is next next: senshuu, konshuu, raishuu, saraishuu.
  • A second sen goes one step further back: sensenshuu is last last week.
  • Years are irregular: ototoshi, kyonen, kotoshi, rainen, sarainen. Last year is kyonen, not sennen.

Ototoi, kinou, ashita and asatte

  • ototoi is the day before yesterday, and kinou is yesterday. ashita is tomorrow, and asatte is the day after tomorrow.
  • kinou and kyou are long sounds: write the u at the end (kinou, kyou).
  • ototoi and ototoshi start the same way. The first is two days back, and the second is two years back.

Morning and night words

  • kesa means this morning. kyou no asa is not used.
  • konban means tonight, and yuube means last night. yuube is the same as kinou no yoru.
  • The mai words mean every: maiasa (every morning), maiban (every night), mainichi (every day).
  • yoru and ban both mean night. ban shows up inside words like konban and maiban.

Nan plus an ending

  • nanji asks the hour, and nanpun asks the minutes. nannichi asks the date, and nanyoubi asks the day of the week.
  • nangatsu asks the month, and nannen asks the year.
  • The word itsu asks when in general, and itsugoro asks around when.

Seasons

  • haru is spring, natsu is summer, aki is autumn and fuyu is winter. kisetsu is the word for season.
  • The book sets the seasons by month: haru is March to May, natsu is June to August, aki is September to November, fuyu is December to February.
  • Winter runs across the new year, so fuyu goes from juunigatsu to nigatsu.
  • Four seasons is yottsu, using the general counter tsu.

Ni with times

  • In A wa Time desu there is no ni: kurasu wa suiyoubi desu.
  • With arimasu, use ni for the time something is held: nichiyoubi ni kurasu ga arimasu.
  • Do not add ni after kinou, kyou, ashita or mainichi. Do not add it after kara, made or goro.

Words with two names

  • Class is jugyou or kurasu, and meeting is kaigi or mi-tingu. Both of each pair are fine.
  • First is mazu or hajime ni. Night is yoru or ban.
  • Yesterday night is yuube or kinou no yoru. Every month is maitsuki or maigetsu.

Yasumi, kyuukei and natsuyasumi

  • The word yasumi means a holiday or vacation. kyuukei is a short break or rest.
  • natsuyasumi is summer vacation, which is natsu plus yasumi.
  • A gakkou no yasumi is a school holiday. A kyuukei is the break between classes.

Part A: Say the clock times

1yoji juugofun (よじ じゅうごふん)4 o'clock is the special reading yoji. 15 minutes is juugofun (it takes fun). The hour comes first.

5sanji juppun (さんじ じゅっぷん)3 o'clock is sanji. 10 minutes is juppun (it takes pun, with a squeezed sound). The hour comes first.
6ichiji ippun (いちじ いっぷん)1 o'clock is ichiji. 1 minute is ippun (it takes pun, with a squeezed sound). The hour comes first.
7rokuji roppun (ろくじ ろっぷん)6 o'clock is rokuji. 6 minutes is roppun (it takes pun, with a squeezed sound). The hour comes first.
8juuniji happun (じゅうにじ はっぷん)12 o'clock is juuniji. 8 minutes is happun (it takes pun, with a squeezed sound). The hour comes first.
9goji nijuppun (ごじ にじゅっぷん)5 o'clock is goji. 20 minutes is nijuppun (it takes pun, with a squeezed sound). The hour comes first.
10shichiji yonjuugofun (しちじ よんじゅうごふん)7 o'clock is the special reading shichiji. 45 minutes is yonjuugofun (it takes fun). The hour comes first.

title: Span of Time
intro: Chapter 5 teaches you to say how long something takes. You move from a point on the clock (4 o'clock) to a length of time (4 hours), and learn the words for minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. Then you use them in sentences: A wa Span of Time desu, how often (ni), about (gurai), from and up to a place (kara, made), before and after (mae, sugi) and by vehicle (de). Finally, you learn the verb kakarimasu for what it takes in time or money, and how to ask with donogurai, the nan question words and ikuragurai.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
5.1 Span of time: a point or a length?

Chapter 4 gave you points in time: yoji is 4 o'clock, sangatsu is March and tooka is the 10th. Chapter 5 gives you lengths of time, which say how long something lasts: yojikan is 4 hours, sankagetsu is 3 months and tookakan is 10 days. You use a length of time to talk about how long a class, a trip or a meeting takes.

Most lengths of time are built by adding an ending. Hours always end in jikan and weeks always end in shuukan, so those two endings never drop. For minutes, days, months and years you may add kan (span), but it is optional: sanpun and sanpunkan both mean 3 minutes. The book writes this as sanpun(kan). Adding kan is a handy way to show that you mean a length and not a date, for example futsukakan (2 days) next to futsuka (the 2nd).

Months change their ending as well. Gatsu names a month on the calendar (sangatsu is March), while kagetsu counts months (sankagetsu is 3 months). Years work the same way: a year name like nisen nijuuyonen (2024) is a point, and yonen is a length of 4 years.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
よじyoji4 o'clock (a point in time)
よじかんyojikan4 hours (a length of time)
さんがつsangatsuMarch (a month on the calendar)
さんかげつsankagetsu3 months (a length of time)
しがつshigatsuApril (a month on the calendar)
よんかげつyonkagetsu4 months (a length of time)

とおかかんtookakan10 days (a length of time)

かいぎは さんじです。kaigi wa sanji desu.The meeting is at 3 o'clock.
かいぎは さんじかんです。kaigi wa sanjikan desu.The meeting is 3 hours long.

5.2 How long: minutes and hours

Minutes use the same endings as the clock minutes in Chapter 4: pun for 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10, and fun for 2, 5, 7 and 9. The numbers 1, 6, 8 and 10 also squeeze the sound before pun: ippun, roppun, happun, juppun. The book lists yonfun next to yonpun, and nanfun next to nanpun, so both forms are fine. Bigger numbers follow their last digit: juugofun is 15 minutes, nijuppun is 20 minutes and yonjuugofun is 45 minutes. The kan after minutes is optional.

Hours are the number plus jikan, and the kan is part of the word, so it never drops: ichijikan is 1 hour and nijikan is 2 hours. The special clock readings carry over: 4 hours is yojikan (not yonjikan) and 9 hours is kujikan (not kyuujikan). For 7 hours you have a choice, nanajikan or shichijikan, unlike the clock time, where only shichiji works. Put han (half) after jikan for a half hour: ichijikan han is 1 hour and a half. Large numbers just work: nijuujikan is 20 hours and hyakujikan is 100 hours.

To ask, use nanpun (how many minutes) and nanjikan (how many hours).

5.3 How long: days and weeks

One day is ichinichi. It is not the same word as tsuitachi, which is the 1st of the month. For 2 to 10 days, you use the same special words as the dates in Chapter 4: futsuka, mikka, yokka, itsuka, muika, nanoka, youka, kokonoka and tooka. The kan after them is optional, but it helps to show that you mean a length: futsuka is the 2nd, and futsukakan is 2 days. From 11 days on, the days are read like the dates from Chapter 4 too, for example juuichinichi (11), juuyokka (14), juugonichi (15), hatsuka (20) and nijuuhachinichi (28). The book's table stops at 15 days, but its translation exercise asks for 28 days, so it is worth knowing that the pattern keeps going. Ask with nannichi (how many days). The book prints the question word as nannichikan in one box.

Weeks are the number plus shuukan, and the kan always stays: isshuukan is 1 week and nishuukan is 2 weeks. The numbers 1, 8 and 10 squeeze the sound: isshuukan, hasshuukan, jusshuukan. Ask with nanshuukan (how many weeks).

5.4 How long: months and years

Months are the number plus kagetsu: nikagetsu is 2 months and sankagetsu is 3 months. The numbers 1, 6, 8 and 10 squeeze the sound: ikkagetsu, rokkagetsu, hakkagetsu and jukkagetsu. For 8 months you can also say hachikagetsu. Six months has a second name, hantoshi (half a year), and one month can also be hitotsuki. From 11 months, put juu in front: juuikkagetsu is 11 months and juunikagetsu is 12 months. The kan is optional. Ask with nankagetsu (how many months).

Years are the number plus nen, and the kan is optional: ichinen, ninen, sannen. Three numbers need care: 4 years is yonen (not yonnen), 7 years is nananen or shichinen, and 9 years is kyuunen. Do not mix these up with the year names from Chapter 4. Nisen nijuuyonen is the year 2024, and yonen is a length of 4 years. Ask with nannen (how many years). The book prints the question word as nannenkan in one box.

5.5 A wa Span of Time desu (bunkei 5.1)

A length of time is a noun, so it can end a copula sentence just like the ones from Chapter 1. The pattern is A wa Span of Time desu, and it says that A lasts that long. A is the thing you are measuring, such as a class, a meeting, a trip or a holiday. Put wa after A and desu after the length of time. No other particle goes in between.

Be careful to pick the right kind of word. Kaigi wa sanji desu uses a point in time, so the meeting is at 3 o'clock. Kaigi wa sanjikan desu uses a length of time, so the meeting lasts 3 hours. The last two rows of the table show the pair side by side.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
クラスは よじかんです。kurasu wa yojikan desu.Class is 4 hours.
かいぎは さんじゅっぷんです。kaigi wa sanjuppun desu.The meeting is 30 minutes.
にほんの ふゆは さんかげつです。nihon no fuyu wa sankagetsu desu.Japan's winter is 3 months.
ゼミは にしゅうかんです。zemi wa nishuukan desu.The seminar is 2 weeks.
トレーニングは みっかかんです。tore-ningu wa mikkakan desu.The training is 3 days.

5.6 Span of Time ni Frequency (bunkei 5.2)

To say how often something happens within a length of time, put ni right after the length of time and then say the number of times with kai. Isshuukan ni gokai is five times a week. Read ni here as per or in each: in one week, five times. The length is usually one unit (ichinichi, isshuukan, ikkagetsu, ichinen), but it can be any length, such as yojikan ni nikai (twice in four hours).

The counter kai (times) comes from Chapter 3: ikkai, nikai, sankai, yonkai, gokai, rokkai and so on. Ask how many times with nankai. The whole phrase can finish a sentence with desu, as in kurasu wa isshuukan ni nikai desu (the class is twice a week). This ni is different from the ni of Chapter 4 that marks the time something happens, so do not mix them up.

5.7 Span of Time gurai (bunkei 5.3)

Add gurai after a length of time to say about or around: ichijikan gurai is about 1 hour. Gurai goes right after the length, and it works with the kan form or the short form, so sanjuppun gurai and sanjuppunkan gurai are both fine. Gurai also goes with amounts of money, which is why it appears in ikuragurai later in this chapter.

For a point in time you use goro from Chapter 4 instead. Shichiji goro is around 7 o'clock, but nanajikan gurai is about 7 hours. A good way to remember it is goro for the clock and gurai for the length.

5.8 Location kara and Location made (bunkei 5.4)

You already know kara (from) and made (until, up to) after times. They also go after places: koujou kara is from the factory and ginkou made is up to the bank. Kara marks the starting point and made marks the end point.

To say how far a place is in time, put the length of time right after the place: su-pa- kara gofun is 5 minutes from the supermarket, and eki made sanjuppun is 30 minutes up to the station. You can also use both in one sentence: ie kara gakkou made juppun desu says that it is 10 minutes from the house to school.

5.9 Span of Time mae and sugi (bunkei 5.5)

Mae means before and sugi means after or past. They follow the time or the length of time directly, with nothing in between. After a clock time and a number of minutes, they say how far a moment is from the hour: ichiji gofun mae is 5 minutes before 1 o'clock, and niji gofun sugi is 5 minutes past 2 o'clock. Say the hour first, then the minutes, then mae or sugi.

After a length of time on its own, mae means ago or early: gofun mae is 5 minutes ago (or 5 minutes early), and ichijikan mae is 1 hour ago. The book only shows sugi with a clock time.

5.10 Mode of transportation de (bunkei 5.6)

Put de after a vehicle to say how you go: basu de is by bus and hikouki de is by airplane. The table lists the vehicles. The one exception is aruite (on foot, by walking). It already means by walking, so it takes no de: aruite gofun desu is 5 minutes on foot.

To mention two vehicles in one trip, join them with to: densha to basu de is by train and bus. The de phrase fits in front of a length of time or an amount: chikatetsu de sanjuppun desu is 30 minutes by subway. The word de also means by or via, so a place can come before it, as in ie kara jitensha de.

5.11 A wa Interrogative desu ka (bunkei 5.7)

To ask how long, use a question word made of nan plus the ending: nanpun (how many minutes), nanjikan (hours), nannichi or nannichikan (days), nanshuukan (weeks), nankagetsu (months) and nannen or nannenkan (years). The general question word is donogurai (how long), and it works for any length of time.

Add ka at the end to turn the sentence into a question: A wa Interrogative desu ka. The answer uses the same sentence with a real length of time: A wa Span of Time desu. Pick the question word that matches the unit you expect in the answer. If you expect hours, ask with nanjikan.

なんじかんnanjikanhow many hours
なんにち(かん)nannichi(kan)how many days
なんしゅうかんnanshuukanhow many weeks

どのぐらいdonoguraihow long (any length of time)
トレーニングは なんしゅうかんですか。tore-ningu wa nanshuukan desu ka.How many weeks is the training?
さんしゅうかんです。sanshuukan desu.3 weeks.
しごとは なんじかんですか。shigoto wa nanjikan desu ka.How many hours is your work?
はちじかんです。hachijikan desu.8 hours.
にほんの ふゆは なんかげつですか。nihon no fuyu wa nankagetsu desu ka.How many months is Japan's winter?
にほんの ふゆは さんかげつです。nihon no fuyu wa sankagetsu desu.Japan's winter is 3 months.
きゅうけいは なんぷんですか。kyuukei wa nanpun desu ka.How many minutes is the break?
きゅうけいは じゅうごふんです。kyuukei wa juugofun desu.The break is 15 minutes.
いっかげつに なんにちかんですか。ikkagetsu ni nannichikan desu ka.How many days a month?
はつかかんです。hatsukakan desu.20 days.
ミーティングは なんじかんですか。mi-tingu wa nanjikan desu ka.How many hours is the meeting?
いちじかんはん ぐらいです。ichijikan han gurai desu.It is about one and a half hours.
でんしゃで なんじかんですか。densha de nanjikan desu ka.How many hours by train?
にじかんです。nijikan desu.2 hours.
だいがくは なんねんかんですか。daigaku wa nannenkan desu ka.How many years is the university?
よねんかんです。yonenkan desu.4 years.

5.12 Span of Time kakarimasu and Cost kakarimasu (bunkei 5.8)

Kakarimasu is a verb. With a length of time it means takes, and with an amount of money it means costs. Put the length or the amount right before it: sanshuukan kakarimasu is it takes 3 weeks, and sen en kakarimasu is it costs 1,000 yen. The thing that takes the time or the money can come first with wa: shiken wa sanjuppun kakarimasu is the exam takes 30 minutes. A place, a vehicle or both can come before the length, as in byouin kara gofun kakarimasu (it takes 5 minutes from the hospital) and basu de kyuufun kakarimasu (it takes 9 minutes by bus).

Notice how this differs from A wa Span of Time desu. Desu says that A is that long. Kakarimasu says that it takes that long. Both fit a class or a meeting. For money, use the number readings from Chapter 3, including the special ones: roppyaku (600), happyaku (800), sanzen (3,000), and sen (1,000) on its own.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
さんしゅうかん かかります。sanshuukan kakarimasu.It takes 3 weeks.
よんじゅうごふん かかります。yonjuugofun kakarimasu.It takes 45 minutes.
びょういんから ごふんかかります。byouin kara gofun kakarimasu.It takes 5 minutes from the hospital.
バスで きゅうふんかかります。basu de kyuufun kakarimasu.It takes 9 minutes by bus.
しけんは さんじゅっぷんかかります。shiken wa sanjuppun kakarimasu.The exam takes 30 minutes.
トレーニングは ごねんかかります。tore-ningu wa gonen kakarimasu.The training takes 5 years.
ミーティングは にじかんかかります。mi-tingu wa nijikan kakarimasu.The meeting takes 2 hours.
クラスは はっかげつかかります。kurasu wa hakkagetsu kakarimasu.The class takes 8 months.
せんえん かかります。sen en kakarimasu.It costs 1,000 yen.
ごまんえん かかります。go man en kakarimasu.It costs 50,000 yen.
いえから がっこうまで ろっぴゃくえん かかります。ie kara gakkou made roppyaku en kakarimasu.It costs 600 yen from the house to school.
バスで ひゃくさんじゅうえん かかります。basu de hyaku san juu en kakarimasu.It costs 130 yen by bus.
しんかんせんで にまんえん かかります。shinkansen de ni man en kakarimasu.It costs 20,000 yen by Shinkansen.
トレーニングは じゅうまんえん かかります。tore-ningu wa juu man en kakarimasu.The training costs 100,000 yen.
きっぷは さんぜんえん かかります。kippu wa sanzen en kakarimasu.The ticket costs 3,000 yen.
かたみちは はっぴゃくえん かかります。katamichi wa happyaku en kakarimasu.One way costs 800 yen.

5.13 A wa donogurai kakarimasu ka (bunkei 5.9)

Donogurai means how long, and it asks about a length of time. Put it in front of kakarimasu ka: donogurai kakarimasu ka asks how long something takes. In A wa donogurai kakarimasu ka, A is the thing that takes the time, such as a meeting or a trip.

You can use the other span question words from lesson 5.11 in the same place, which gives Interrogative Noun kakarimasu ka: nanjikan kakarimasu ka asks how many hours it takes. Donogurai is the open question, and words like nanjikan are more exact. Answer with a length of time and kakarimasu, such as juugofun kakarimasu or ichijikan gurai kakarimasu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
どのぐらいかかりますか。donogurai kakarimasu ka.How long does it take?
ミーティングは どのぐらいかかりますか。mi-tingu wa donogurai kakarimasu ka.How long is the meeting?
タクシーで どのぐらいかかりますか。takushi- de donogurai kakarimasu ka.How long does it take by taxi?
しけんは なんじかんかかりますか。shiken wa nanjikan kakarimasu ka.How many hours is the exam?
かいぎは なんぷんかかりますか。kaigi wa nanpun kakarimasu ka.How many minutes is the meeting?
なんねんかんかかりますか。nannenkan kakarimasu ka.How many years does it take?
トレーニングは なんねんかかりますか。tore-ningu wa nannen kakarimasu ka.How many years is the training?
クラスは なんかげつかかりますか。kurasu wa nankagetsu kakarimasu ka.How many months is the class?
じゅうごふんかかります。juugofun kakarimasu.It takes 15 minutes.
いちじかん ぐらいかかります。ichijikan gurai kakarimasu.It takes about an hour.

5.14 A wa ikuragurai kakarimasu ka (bunkei 5.10)

To ask about money with kakarimasu, use ikura (how much) or ikuragurai (about how much). Ikuragurai is the softer question, because it only asks for an estimate. The book's contents page lists the patterns up to bunkei 5.9, but the pages teach this tenth pattern, so it is included here.

Donogurai asks about time and ikura or ikuragurai asks about money, even though both end in kakarimasu ka. The answer is an amount in yen followed by kakarimasu: ni man en kakarimasu. Remember that the book sometimes writes ikuragurai as two words, ikura gurai.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
にほんから いくらかかりますか。nihon kara ikura kakarimasu ka.How much does it cost from Japan?
けいたいは いくらかかりますか。keitai wa ikura kakarimasu ka.How much will a cell phone cost?
バスで いくらぐらいかかりますか。basu de ikuragurai kakarimasu ka.Around how much will it cost by bus?
しんかんせんで いくらかかりますか。shinkansen de ikura kakarimasu ka.How much will it cost by Shinkansen?
かたみちは いくらかかりますか。katamichi wa ikura kakarimasu ka.How much will it cost for a one-way trip?
でんしゃで いくらかかりますか。densha de ikura kakarimasu ka.How much will it cost by train?
いえまで いくらかかりますか。ie made ikura kakarimasu ka.How much up to your house?
かいしゃから いくらかかりますか。kaisha kara ikura kakarimasu ka.How much from the company?
バスで ひゃくさんじゅうえん かかります。basu de hyaku san juu en kakarimasu.It costs 130 yen by bus.
おうふくは せんろっぴゃくえん かかります。oufuku wa sen roppyaku en kakarimasu.A roundtrip costs 1,600 yen.

5.15 Putting it together: from, until, by and how long

This last lesson is an extra that pulls the earlier ones into longer sentences, because the exercises need them. The usual order is the starting place with kara, the end place with made, the vehicle with de, and then the length of time or the cost with kakarimasu. You can leave out any part you do not need.

To answer How long does it take?, use a length of time (and gurai if you are not sure): ie kara eki made basu de sanjuppun kakarimasu. To answer How much does it cost?, use an amount of money. The question words follow the same order: ie kara eki made basu de donogurai kakarimasu ka asks about time, and ie kara eki made basu de ikura kakarimasu ka asks about money.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
いえから えきまで バスで さんじゅっぷんかかります。ie kara eki made basu de sanjuppun kakarimasu.It takes 30 minutes by bus from my house to the station.
いえから がっこうまで あるいて じゅっぷんです。ie kara gakkou made aruite juppun desu.It is 10 minutes on foot from my house to school.
にほんから かんこくまで ひこうきで にじかんぐらいかかります。nihon kara kankoku made hikouki de nijikan gurai kakarimasu.It takes about 2 hours by airplane from Japan to Korea.
かいしゃから いえまで どのぐらいかかりますか。kaisha kara ie made donogurai kakarimasu ka.How long does it take from the company to your house?
かいしゃから いえまで ちかてつで いくらぐらいかかりますか。kaisha kara ie made chikatetsu de ikuragurai kakarimasu ka.Around how much does it cost by subway from the company to your house?
おおさかから とうきょうまで しんかんせんで さんじかんぐらいです。oosaka kara toukyou made shinkansen de sanjikan gurai desu.It is about 3 hours from Osaka to Tokyo by Shinkansen.
いえから デパートまで じてんしゃで じゅうごふんかかります。ie kara depa-to made jitensha de juugofun kakarimasu.It takes 15 minutes by bicycle from my house to the department store.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Point or length

  • yoji is 4 o'clock, but yojikan is 4 hours. The ending kan turns a point into a length.
  • sangatsu is March, but sankagetsu is 3 months. shigatsu is April, but yonkagetsu is 4 months.
  • tooka is the 10th, but tookakan is 10 days.
  • A year name like nisen nijuuyonen (2024) is a point. yonen is a length of 4 years.
  • kaigi wa sanji desu says the meeting is at 3 o'clock. kaigi wa sanjikan desu says it lasts 3 hours.

When you need kan

  • Hours always keep jikan (ichijikan), and weeks always keep shuukan (isshuukan).
  • Minutes, days, months and years can drop kan. sanpun, mikka, sankagetsu and sannen are fine on their own.
  • Add kan when you want to be clear that you mean a length. futsuka is the 2nd, and futsukakan is 2 days.

Hours: 4, 7 and 9

  • 4 hours is yojikan and 9 hours is kujikan, just like the clock times yoji and kuji. Do not say yonjikan or kyuujikan.
  • 7 hours can be nanajikan or shichijikan. The clock time 7 o'clock is only shichiji.
  • ichijikan han is 1 hour and a half. ichiji han is 1:30 on the clock. han goes at the end in both.

Fun or pun in lengths

  • The rules are the same as in Chapter 4. 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 take pun, and 2, 5, 7 and 9 take fun.
  • 1, 6, 8 and 10 also squeeze the sound: ippun, roppun, happun, juppun.
  • Both yonpun and yonfun are fine for 4 minutes, and both nanpun and nanfun are fine for how many minutes.
  • Bigger numbers follow the last digit: juugofun (15), nijuppun (20), yonjuugofun (45).

Days: dates or lengths

  • futsuka is both the 2nd and 2 days. The same goes for mikka, yokka, itsuka and the other words up to tooka.
  • One day is ichinichi, but the 1st is tsuitachi.
  • From 11 days on, use the date words from Chapter 4: juuyokka (14 days), hatsuka (20 days), nijuuhachinichi (28 days).
  • Add kan to be sure the listener hears a length: mikkakan is 3 days.

Itsuka and itsu

  • itsuka is 5 days (or the 5th), and itsu means when. They look alike but they are different words.
  • itsukakan is 5 days. itsu desu ka asks when.

Weeks

  • The squeezed sound shows up for 1, 8 and 10: isshuukan, hasshuukan, jusshuukan. The other weeks do not squeeze: nishuukan, sanshuukan.
  • One week is isshuukan, but this week is konshuu from Chapter 4. Lengths use shuukan and names like this week use shuu.

Gatsu or kagetsu

  • gatsu names a month, and kagetsu counts months. rokugatsu is June, but rokkagetsu is 6 months.
  • ichigatsu is January, but ikkagetsu is 1 month.
  • hantoshi (half a year) means the same as rokkagetsu.
  • 1, 6, 8 and 10 squeeze the sound: ikkagetsu, rokkagetsu, hakkagetsu, jukkagetsu.

Years: names and lengths

  • 4 years is yonen, not yonnen. 7 years is nananen or shichinen. 9 years is kyuunen.
  • A year name from Chapter 4 says which year, and a length says how many years. nisen nijuuyonen is the year 2024, but yonen is 4 years.

Gurai or goro

  • goro goes with a point in time: shichiji goro is around 7 o'clock.
  • gurai goes with a length: ichijikan gurai is about 1 hour. It also goes with money: ikuragurai.
  • Do not say shichiji gurai or ichijikan goro.

Ni after a length or after a time

  • isshuukan ni nikai uses ni to mean per or in each. It is followed by a number of times.
  • nichiyoubi ni kurasu ga arimasu uses ni to say when something happens.
  • kinou, kyou, ashita and mainichi take no ni at all.

Kai for times and kai for floors

  • Both words are read kai, but the floor forms differ from the times forms. 3 times is sankai, but the 3rd floor is sangai.
  • 2 times and the 2nd floor are the same word, nikai. Context tells you which one.

Kara and made with places

  • kara marks the starting place and made marks the end place. eki kara is from the station, and eki made is up to the station.
  • The length of time comes right after the place: eki made sanjuppun is 30 minutes up to the station.
  • With times, kara and made work the same way: gogo niji kara goji made.

Mae, made and sugi

  • mae means before, and made means until. They sound alike, so check the meaning.
  • mae also means in front of, as in eki no mae from Chapter 2. After a time it means before.
  • sugi means after or past: niji gofun sugi is 5 minutes past 2.
  • mae and sugi come after the whole time. Say ichiji gofun mae, not gofun mae ichiji.

Mae with a time and mae with a length

  • ichiji gofun mae is 5 minutes before 1 o'clock. It names a moment.
  • gofun mae on its own is 5 minutes ago, or 5 minutes early.

De and aruite

  • Put de after a vehicle: basu de is by bus, and hikouki de is by airplane.
  • aruite already means on foot, so it takes no de.
  • To name two vehicles, join them with to: densha to basu de is by train and bus.

Kakarimasu: time or money

  • kakarimasu works for both time and money: ichijikan kakarimasu takes 1 hour, and sen en kakarimasu costs 1,000 yen.
  • kurasu wa yojikan desu says the class is 4 hours. kurasu wa yojikan kakarimasu says the class takes 4 hours.
  • The question tells you which one is meant. donogurai asks about time, and ikura asks about money.

Donogurai, ikura and ikuragurai

  • donogurai asks how long. ikura asks how much, and ikuragurai asks around how much.
  • nanjikan asks for hours only, but donogurai can be answered with any length.
  • ikura also asks a price in Chapter 3: kippu wa ikura desu ka.

Nan questions

  • Pick the question word by the unit you want back: nanpun, nanjikan, nannichi, nanshuukan, nankagetsu, nannen.
  • nanji asks the time on the clock, but nanjikan asks how many hours.
  • nangatsu asks which month, but nankagetsu asks how many months.

Money amounts with kakarimasu

  • 1,000 yen is sen en, not ichisen en. 3,000 yen is sanzen en and 8,000 yen is hassen en.
  • 600 yen is roppyaku en and 800 yen is happyaku en.
  • 20,000 yen is ni man en, as in Chapter 3.

Oufuku and katamichi

  • oufuku is a roundtrip, and katamichi is one way.
  • If a roundtrip costs 3,000 yen, one way costs half of that, 1,500 yen.

Student words

  • gakusei is the general word for a student.
  • seito is a pupil in a class, and ryuugakusei is a student studying abroad.
  • kurasumeito is a classmate, and menba- is a member of a group.

Katakana long vowels

  • takushi-, menba-, guru-pu, tore-ningu and o-tobai use a hyphen for the long sound.
  • Hiragana words double the vowel instead: hikouki, ryuugakusei, shukudai.

Words with two names

  • o-tobai or baiku is a motorcycle. jidousha or kuruma is a car.
  • hakkagetsu or hachikagetsu is 8 months. nanajikan or shichijikan is 7 hours.
  • yonpun or yonfun is 4 minutes. rokkagetsu or hantoshi is 6 months.

Yasumi, hiruyasumi and kyuukei

  • yasumi is a holiday or vacation. hiruyasumi is a lunch break, from hiru (noon) and yasumi.
  • kyuukei is a short break, such as the one between classes.

10nihongo no kurasu wa nankagetsu desu ka. [にほんごのクラスは なんかげつ ですか。]

Translation (page 85)

Translate into Japanese.

#QuestionYour answer
1The company seminar is 4 hours.

7How many hours is the meeting?

sections.title: Answer key
sections.html:
Part A: Say how long: minutes

#AnswerWhy
1ippun (いっぷん)One minute is ippun. After 1, pun gets a squeezed sound.
2sanpun (さんぷん)Three takes pun: sanpun.
3yonpun / yonfun (よんぷん / よんふん)Four takes pun, and the book also lists yonfun. The kan after minutes is optional.
4roppun (ろっぷん)Six takes pun with a squeezed sound: roppun.
5happun (はっぷん)Eight takes pun with a squeezed sound: happun.
6juppun (じゅっぷん)Ten takes pun with a squeezed sound: juppun.
7juunifun (じゅうにふん)juu (10) plus nifun (2). Two takes fun.
8nijuppun (にじゅっぷん)ni juu (20) plus the squeezed pun: nijuppun.
9sanjuppun (さんじゅっぷん)san juu (30) plus the squeezed pun: sanjuppun.
10yonjuugofun (よんじゅうごふん)yon juu (40) plus gofun (5). Five takes fun.
11nanpun / nanfun (なんぷん / なんふん)nan plus pun or fun. The book accepts both.

Part B: Say how long: hours

#AnswerWhy
1ichijikan (いちじかん)The number plus jikan. The kan is part of the word for hours.
2nijikan (にじかん)The number plus jikan: nijikan.
3yojikan (よじかん)Special reading: yojikan, not yonjikan.
4rokujikan (ろくじかん)The number plus jikan: rokujikan.
5nanajikan / shichijikan (ななじかん / しちじかん)Both are fine for lengths. The clock time 7 o'clock is only shichiji.
6kujikan (くじかん)Special reading: kujikan, not kyuujikan.
7juujikan (じゅうじかん)Ten is juu, so juu plus jikan is juujikan.
8nijuujikan (にじゅうじかん)ni juu (20) plus jikan.
9hyakujikan (ひゃくじかん)hyaku (100) plus jikan.
10ichijikan han (いちじかんはん)han (half) goes after jikan.
11nijikan han (にじかんはん)nijikan (2 hours) plus han (half).
12nanjikan (なんじかん)nan plus jikan.

Part C: Say how long: days

#AnswerWhy
1ichinichi (いちにち)One day is ichinichi. The 1st of the month is a different word, tsuitachi.
2futsuka (ふつか)2 days uses the same word as the date: futsuka. Adding kan (futsukakan) is also fine.
3mikka (みっか)3 days uses the same word as the date: mikka. Adding kan (mikkakan) is also fine.
4itsuka (いつか)5 days uses the same word as the date: itsuka. Adding kan (itsukakan) is also fine.
5muika (むいか)6 days uses the same word as the date: muika. Adding kan (muikakan) is also fine.
6youka (ようか)8 days uses the same word as the date: youka. Adding kan (youkakan) is also fine.
7tooka (とおか)10 days uses the same word as the date: tooka. Adding kan (tookakan) is also fine.
8juugonichi (じゅうごにち)The number plus nichi: juugonichi. It is read like the 15th. kan is optional.
9hatsuka (はつか)The 20th has its own word, hatsuka, and it is used for 20 days too.
10nijuuhachinichi (にじゅうはちにち)ni juu (20) plus hachi (8) plus nichi: nijuuhachinichi. It is read like the 28th.
11nannichi / nannichikan (なんにち / なんにちかん)nan plus nichi. The book also prints nannichikan.

Part D: Say how long: weeks

#AnswerWhy
1isshuukan (いっしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan, with a squeezed sound for 1: isshuukan.
2nishuukan (にしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan: nishuukan. The kan always stays for weeks.
3sanshuukan (さんしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan: sanshuukan. The kan always stays for weeks.
4yonshuukan (よんしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan: yonshuukan. The kan always stays for weeks.
5hasshuukan (はっしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan, with a squeezed sound for 8: hasshuukan.
6jusshuukan (じゅっしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan, with a squeezed sound for 10: jusshuukan.
7nanshuukan (なんしゅうかん)nan plus shuukan.

Part E: Say how long: months

#AnswerWhy
1ikkagetsu (いっかげつ)The number plus kagetsu, with a squeezed sound after 1: ikkagetsu.
2nikagetsu (にかげつ)The number plus kagetsu: nikagetsu.
3sankagetsu (さんかげつ)The number plus kagetsu: sankagetsu.
4yonkagetsu (よんかげつ)Four takes yon here: yonkagetsu.
5rokkagetsu / hantoshi (ろっかげつ / はんとし)rokkagetsu has a squeezed sound. hantoshi (half a year) means the same.
6hakkagetsu / hachikagetsu (はっかげつ / はちかげつ)hakkagetsu squeezes the sound. hachikagetsu is also fine.
7jukkagetsu (じゅっかげつ)Ten squeezes the sound: jukkagetsu.
8hantoshi (はんとし)hantoshi is its own word and equals rokkagetsu (6 months).
9juunikagetsu (じゅうにかげつ)juu (10) plus nikagetsu (2 months).
10nankagetsu (なんかげつ)nan plus kagetsu.

Part F: Say how long: years

#AnswerWhy
1ichinen (いちねん)The number plus nen: ichinen.
2ninen (にねん)The number plus nen: ninen.
3sannen (さんねん)The number plus nen: sannen.
4yonen (よねん)Special reading: yonen, not yonnen.
5gonen (ごねん)The number plus nen: gonen.
6nananen / shichinen (ななねん / しちねん)Both nananen and shichinen are fine for lengths.
7kyuunen (きゅうねん)Nine is kyuu here: kyuunen.
8juunen (じゅうねん)Ten is juu, so juu plus nen is juunen.
9juugonen (じゅうごねん)juu (10) plus go (5) plus nen.
10nannen (なんねん)nan plus nen. The book also prints nannenkan.

Part G: Say these lengths of time (the book's drill)

#AnswerWhy
1sanjuppun (さんじゅっぷん)san juu (30) plus the squeezed pun: sanjuppun.
2yonshuukan (よんしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan: yonshuukan.
3nikagetsu (にかげつ)The number plus kagetsu: nikagetsu.
4ichijikan han (いちじかんはん)ichijikan (1 hour) plus han (half).
5muika (むいか)Special day word: muika. The form muikakan also works.
6yokka (よっか)Special day word: yokka. yokkakan also works.
7ichinichi (いちにち)One day is ichinichi.
8nijuujikan (にじゅうじかん)ni juu (20) plus jikan.
9isshuukan (いっしゅうかん)The squeezed sound after 1: isshuukan.
10nishuukan (にしゅうかん)The number plus shuukan: nishuukan.
11ikkagetsu (いっかげつ)The squeezed sound after 1: ikkagetsu.
12yonkagetsu (よんかげつ)Four takes yon here: yonkagetsu.
13hachinen (はちねん)The number plus nen: hachinen.
14juugonen (じゅうごねん)juu (10) plus go (5) plus nen.

Part H: Point or length? Say both

#AnswerWhy
1yoji, yojikan (よじ、よじかん)4 o'clock is yoji. Adding kan gives the length yojikan. Both use the special reading yo.
2sanji, sanjikan (さんじ、さんじかん)sanji is the clock time. sanjikan is the length.
3kuji, kujikan (くじ、くじかん)Both use the special reading ku.
4sangatsu, sankagetsu (さんがつ、さんかげつ)gatsu names the month. kagetsu counts months.
5shigatsu, yonkagetsu (しがつ、よんかげつ)April is the special reading shigatsu. 4 months is yonkagetsu.
6rokugatsu, rokkagetsu (ろくがつ、ろっかげつ)gatsu names the month, and kagetsu counts months with a squeezed sound after 6.
7tooka, tookakan (とおか、とおかかん)The same word. Adding kan makes it clear that you mean a length.
8nisen nijuuyonen, yonen (にせんにじゅうよねん、よねん)A year name is read like a big number plus nen. A length of 4 years is yonen.

9kyuukei wa juppun desu. (きゅうけいは じゅっぷんです。)Ten minutes is juppun.
10daigaku wa yonen desu. (だいがくは よねんです。)Four years is the special reading yonen.

9arubaito wa isshuukan ni nikai desu. (アルバイトは いっしゅうかんに にかいです。)A wa Span ni Frequency desu.
10kaigi wa ikkagetsu ni nankai desu ka. (かいぎは いっかげつに なんかいですか。)nankai asks how many times.

title: Adjectives
intro: Chapter 6 teaches you to describe things with adjectives. There are two types, i-adjectives (takai) and na-adjectives (kirei), and you learn the 21 basic pairs of opposites. Then you use adjectives in front of a noun (takai tatemono, kirei na heya), join two adjectives (akarukute hiroi, kirei de yasashii), and change them for the negative and past (takakunai, takakatta, kirei ja arimasen, kirei deshita). You also learn to ask with dou and donna, and to say very, a little and not very with totemo, taihen, chotto and amari.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
6.1 Nouns in the past tense (noun conjugation)

Chapter 6 opens with a quick review of nouns, because the adjective endings you are about to learn borrow them. A noun sentence (A wa B desu) can be present or past, and positive or negative, which gives four forms. The book shows them with shain (employee): desu, dewa arimasen or ja arimasen, deshita, and dewa arimasen deshita or ja arimasen deshita.

To change a noun sentence to the past, only the end changes. Desu becomes deshita, and ja arimasen becomes ja arimasen deshita (just add deshita). Ja is the short form of dewa and both mean the same, so every ja arimasen can also be dewa arimasen. The book prints both in its tables and uses ja arimasen in its drills, so this chapter does too.

The past tense says that something was true earlier: kayoubi wa shiken deshita means Tuesday was the exam. Keep this pattern in mind, because na-adjectives are conjugated in exactly the same way (lesson 6.7).

しゃいんでした。shain deshita.was an employee (past positive)

たなかさんは わたしの がくせいです。tanaka san wa watashi no gakusei desu.Tanaka is my student.
たなかさんは わたしの がくせいでした。tanaka san wa watashi no gakusei deshita.Tanaka was my student.
おかあさんは いしゃです。okaasan wa isha desu.My mother is a doctor.
おかあさんは いしゃでした。okaasan wa isha deshita.My mother was a doctor.
すずきさんは せんせいじゃありません。suzuki san wa sensei ja arimasen.Mr. Suzuki is not a teacher.
すずきさんは せんせいじゃありませんでした。suzuki san wa sensei ja arimasen deshita.Mr. Suzuki was not a teacher.
ジョンさんは けんしゅうせいじゃありません。jon san wa kenshuusei ja arimasen.John is not a trainee.
ジョンさんは けんしゅうせいじゃありませんでした。jon san wa kenshuusei ja arimasen deshita.John was not a trainee.
ADZの しゃいんじゃありませんでした。ADZ no shain ja arimasen deshita.(I) was not an ADZ employee.

6.2 Two types of adjectives: i and na (bunkei 6.1)

Adjectives describe things: a big room, a famous park, a kind teacher. Japanese has two kinds, and almost everything else in this chapter depends on knowing which kind a word is.

The first kind is the i-adjective (written い-adjective). It ends in the sound i: takai (expensive), ookii (big), tanoshii (enjoyable). That last i is the part that changes when you make the word negative or past, as you will see in lesson 6.6.

The second kind is the na-adjective (written な-adjective). It ends in other sounds, and it needs na only when it sits directly in front of a noun: kirei na heya (a clean room), iroiro na mondai (various problems). The book's word lists show this by writing (na) after the word, for example kantan(na). Before desu the na is dropped: heya wa kirei desu means the room is clean.

Here is the trap. Kirei (clean, beautiful) and yuumei (famous) end in i, but they are na-adjectives. Sound alone cannot tell you the type, so learn the type together with each new word and look for the (na) mark. It matters because i-adjectives change their own ending (takai, takakunai, takakatta), while na-adjectives stay the same and only desu changes (kirei desu, kirei deshita).

あぶないabunaidangerous (i-adjective)
やさしいyasashiikind, easy (i-adjective)
いろいろ(な)iroiro(na)various (na-adjective)
りっぱ(な)rippa(na)splendid (na-adjective)
ゆうめい(な)yuumei(na)famous (na-adjective)
やさしい せんせいyasashii senseia kind teacher (i-adjective, no change before a noun)
ゆうめいな せんせいyuumei na senseia famous teacher (na-adjective, na before a noun)
せんせいは やさしいです。sensei wa yasashii desu.The teacher is kind.
せんせいは ゆうめいです。sensei wa yuumei desu.The teacher is famous. (no na before desu)
きれいな へやkirei na heyaa clean room (kirei is a na-adjective)
たのしい しごとtanoshii shigotoan enjoyable job
りっぱな たてものrippa na tatemonoa splendid building

6.3 Basic adjective pairs (bunkei 6.1)

The book teaches adjectives in 21 pairs of opposites. Learn each pair together, because if you remember one half, the other half comes almost for free. Each row shows both words and their types, where i means i-adjective and na means na-adjective.

Most pairs are i + i. The mixed pairs are kantan(na) with muzukashii, kirei(na) with kitanai and hima(na) with isogashii. The pairs where both words are na-adjectives are shizuka(na) with nigiyaka(na), and benri(na) with fuben(na).

Three words show up in more than one pair. Takai means expensive (opposite yasui) and also high or tall (opposite hikui). Atsui is the busiest word: it means hot to the touch (opposite tsumetai), hot weather (opposite samui) and thick (opposite usui). Only the situation and the opposite tell you which meaning is meant. Finally, ii and yoi both mean good. They are the same word, but yoi takes over when you conjugate, which lesson 6.6 explains.

おもい / かるいomoi / karuiheavy / light (i + i)
おもしろい / つまらないomoshiroi / tsumaranaiinteresting, funny / boring (i + i)
ひろい / せまいhiroi / semaiwide / narrow (i + i)
きれい(な) / きたないkirei(na) / kitanaiclean, beautiful / dirty (na + i)
あたらしい / ふるいatarashii / furuinew / old (i + i)
あかるい / くらいakarui / kuraibright / dark (i + i)
しずか(な) / にぎやか(な)shizuka(na) / nigiyaka(na)quiet / lively (na + na)
たかい / やすいtakai / yasuiexpensive / cheap (i + i)
たかい / ひくいtakai / hikuihigh, tall / low (i + i)
ひま(な) / いそがしいhima(na) / isogashiifree / busy (na + i)
べんり(な) / ふべん(な)benri(na) / fuben(na)convenient / inconvenient (na + na)
いい(よい) / わるいii (yoi) / waruigood / bad (i + i)
あつい / つめたいatsui / tsumetaihot (things) / cold (things) (i + i)
あつい / さむいatsui / samuihot (weather) / cold (weather) (i + i)

6.4 Adjective + noun (bunkei 6.2)

The main job of an adjective is to describe a noun, and it goes right in front of the noun. With an i-adjective nothing changes: yasashii sensei (a kind teacher), takai jitensha (an expensive bicycle). With a na-adjective you add na between the adjective and the noun: kirei na heya (a clean room), kantan na shiken (an easy exam). The book calls this Adjective + Noun / Noun Phrase, which tells you that the thing being described can also be a longer phrase, like takai tatemono (a tall building).

Compare two ways of using the same adjective. Heya wa kirei desu says the room is clean. The adjective ends the sentence, so there is no na. Kirei na heya desu says it is a clean room. The adjective sits in front of a noun, so na is needed. Iroiro(na) works the same way and always shows up as iroiro na before a noun: iroiro na mondai (various problems).

You can put the whole phrase anywhere a noun fits, for example before desu or before ga arimasu: ie no chikaku ni ookii kouen ga arimasu.

やさしい せんせいyasashii senseikind teacher

むずかしい じmuzukashii jidifficult letter, difficult character
いろいろな もんだいiroiro na mondaivarious problems
うすい ほんusui honthin book
あかるい ところakarui tokorobright place
きれいな へやkirei na heyaclean room
かんたんな しけんkantan na shikeneasy examination
たかい たてものtakai tatemonotall building
おおきい くるまookii kurumabig car
あたらしい カメラatarashii kameranew camera

へやは きれいです。heya wa kirei desu.The room is clean.
きれいな へやです。kirei na heya desu.It is a clean room.
これは たかい じてんしゃです。kore wa takai jitensha desu.This is an expensive bicycle.
いえの ちかくに おおきい こうえんが あります。ie no chikaku ni ookii kouen ga arimasu.There is a big park near my house.

6.5 Adjective + adjective: kute and de (bunkei 6.3)

The second job of an adjective is to connect to another adjective, as in big and heavy. The first adjective changes shape, and the last one keeps its normal form.

With an i-adjective, drop the final i and add kute: atarashii becomes atarashikute, so atarashikute takai means new and expensive. With a na-adjective, drop the na and add de: nigiyaka(na) becomes nigiyaka de, so nigiyaka de rippa na means lively and splendid. The same chains work in front of a noun, as in atsukute omoi hon (a thick, heavy book). When the last adjective is a na-adjective in front of a noun, it keeps its na: kirei de shizuka na tokoro (a clean, quiet place).

Only the last adjective carries desu and the tense. Say kono heya wa akarukute hiroi desu for This room is bright and wide, and put only the last word in the past: akarukute hirokatta desu. Ii (good) uses its other form here: yokute yasui means good and cheap.

In practice, join qualities that go together in mood, such as akarukute hiroi (bright and wide) or muzukashikute tsumaranai (difficult and boring). Joining a good point with a bad point needs a different word, which this chapter does not cover.

6.6 I-adjectives: present, past and negative (adjective conjugation)

With i-adjectives, the adjective itself changes for negative and past, and desu stays as the polite ending. Take the final i off and add kunai for the negative, katta for the past, and kunakatta for the past negative. So takai (expensive) gives takakunai (not expensive), takakatta (was expensive) and takakunakatta (was not expensive).

The book writes desu in brackets in its tables, because it can be dropped in casual speech. This whole book uses the polite style, so keep desu: takakatta desu. Do not change desu to deshita after an i-adjective. Takai deshita is wrong, and takakatta desu is right.

Ii (good) is the only irregular adjective. It cannot be conjugated, so its other form yoi takes over: yokunai (not good), yokatta (was good) and yokunakatta (was not good). Never say iikunai or iikatta. Also watch tsumaranai (boring). It ends in nai, but it is a normal i-adjective, so its negative is tsumaranakunai (not boring), and its past is tsumaranakatta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
つよいです。tsuyoi desu.is strong (present positive)
つよくないです。tsuyokunai desu.is not strong (present negative)
つよかったです。tsuyokatta desu.was strong (past positive)
つよくなかったです。tsuyokunakatta desu.was not strong (past negative)
いいです。 / よいです。ii desu. / yoi desu.is good (present positive)
よくないです。yokunai desu.is not good (present negative)
よかったです。yokatta desu.was good (past positive)
よくなかったです。yokunakatta desu.was not good (past negative)
おおきいです。ookii desu.is big
おおきくないです。ookikunai desu.is not big
おおきかったです。ookikatta desu.was big
おおきくなかったです。ookikunakatta desu.was not big
つまらないです。tsumaranai desu.is boring
つまらなくないです。tsumaranakunai desu.is not boring
つまらなかったです。tsumaranakatta desu.was boring
つまらなくなかったです。tsumaranakunakatta desu.was not boring
ぎんこうは ちかいです。ginkou wa chikai desu.The bank is near.
ぎんこうは ちかくないです。ginkou wa chikakunai desu.The bank is not near.
ぎんこうは ちかかったです。ginkou wa chikakatta desu.The bank was near.
しけんは むずかしかったです。shiken wa muzukashikatta desu.The exam was difficult.
きのうは あつくなかったです。kinou wa atsukunakatta desu.It was not hot yesterday.

6.7 Na-adjectives: present, past and negative (adjective conjugation)

A na-adjective does not change at all. It is conjugated like a noun, so only the ending after it changes: kirei desu (is clean), kirei ja arimasen (is not clean), kirei deshita (was clean) and kirei ja arimasen deshita (was not clean). You can swap ja for dewa in the negative forms, as the book does in its hima examples.

The na never appears in these four forms, because na is only needed in front of a noun. Say kirei desu, not kirei na desu. This also explains why kirei, which ends in i, is not conjugated like an i-adjective. Never say kirekunai. The negative of kirei is kirei ja arimasen.

Compare the two types side by side. An i-adjective changes its own ending, as in takai, takakunai, takakatta, takakunakatta. A na-adjective stays put, and the endings desu, ja arimasen, deshita and ja arimasen deshita do the work.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
きれいです。kirei desu.is clean (present positive)
きれいではありません。 / きれいじゃありません。kirei dewa arimasen. / kirei ja arimasen.is not clean (present negative)
きれいでした。kirei deshita.was clean (past positive)
きれいではありませんでした。 / きれいじゃありませんでした。kirei dewa arimasen deshita. / kirei ja arimasen deshita.was not clean (past negative)
ひまです。hima desu.is free
ひまではありません。hima dewa arimasen.is not free
ひまでした。hima deshita.was free
ひまではありませんでした。hima dewa arimasen deshita.was not free
べんりです。benri desu.is convenient
べんりじゃありません。benri ja arimasen.is not convenient
べんりでした。benri deshita.was convenient
べんりじゃありませんでした。benri ja arimasen deshita.was not convenient
へやは しずかでした。heya wa shizuka deshita.The room was quiet.
どようびは ひまじゃありませんでした。doyoubi wa hima ja arimasen deshita.I was not free on Saturday.
このみせは べんりじゃありません。kono mise wa benri ja arimasen.This shop is not convenient.
せんせいは ゆうめいじゃありませんでした。sensei wa yuumei ja arimasen deshita.The teacher was not famous.

6.8 How is it? Dou desu ka and donna A desu ka (bunkei 6.4)

Two question words ask about adjectives. Dou means how, and it asks for a description: A wa dou desu ka means How is A? Donna plus a noun means what kind of, and it asks what sort of thing or person something is: donna A desu ka means What kind of A is it? Both questions are always answered with adjectives.

Use dou at the end of the sentence, as in nihongo no kurasu wa dou desu ka, and answer with A wa adjective desu. Use donna directly in front of a noun, as in tanaka san wa donna hito desu ka, and answer with an adjective plus the same noun: yasashii hito desu. For a past question, change desu to deshita: kinou no ryouri wa dou deshita ka (How was the dish yesterday?). The answer then uses a past adjective, for example oishikatta desu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
にほんの でんしゃは どうですか。nihon no densha wa dou desu ka.How is the train in Japan?
べんりです。benri desu.It is convenient.
たなかさんは どんな ひとですか。tanaka san wa donna hito desu ka.What kind of person is Mr. Tanaka?
やさしい ひとです。yasashii hito desu.He is a kind person.
にほんごの クラスは どうですか。nihongo no kurasu wa dou desu ka.How is the Japanese class?
ちょっと むずかしいです。chotto muzukashii desu.It is a little difficult.
このりょうりは どうですか。kono ryouri wa dou desu ka.How is this dish?
とても おいしいです。totemo oishii desu.It is very delicious.
どんな たてものですか。donna tatemono desu ka.What kind of building is it?
たかい たてものです。takai tatemono desu.It is a tall building.
どんな くにですか。donna kuni desu ka.What kind of country is it?
きれいな くにです。kirei na kuni desu.It is a beautiful country.
あたらしい くつは どうですか。atarashii kutsu wa dou desu ka.How are the new shoes?
とても かるいです。totemo karui desu.They are very light.
どんな かばんですか。donna kaban desu ka.What kind of bag is it?
おおきい かばんです。ookii kaban desu.It is a big bag.
きのうの りょうりは どうでしたか。kinou no ryouri wa dou deshita ka.How was the dish yesterday?

6.9 Very: taihen and totemo (bunkei 6.5)

Taihen and totemo both mean very. Put either one directly in front of the adjective and leave everything else alone: yasashii desu becomes taihen yasashii desu, and takai desu becomes totemo takai desu. They also work in the past (totemo atsukatta desu), and in front of a noun phrase (totemo kirei na kuni).

The book treats the two words as the same. Totemo is the one you will hear most in everyday talk, and taihen sounds a little more formal. Both go with positive adjectives only. To say not very, use amari with a negative ending, which comes in the next lesson.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
にほんは とても きれいな くにです。nihon wa totemo kirei na kuni desu.Japan is a very beautiful country.
せんせいは たいへん やさしいです。sensei wa taihen yasashii desu.The teacher is very kind.
そのとけいは とても たかいです。sono tokei wa totemo takai desu.That watch is very expensive.
あしたは たいへん いそがしいです。ashita wa taihen isogashii desu.I am very busy tomorrow.
このくだものは とても やすいです。kono kudamono wa totemo yasui desu.This fruit is very cheap.
わたしの いえは とても とおいです。watashi no ie wa totemo tooi desu.My house is very far.
きょうは とても あついです。kyou wa totemo atsui desu.It is very hot today.
ともだちは とても しずかです。tomodachi wa totemo shizuka desu.My friend is very quiet.
きのうは とても あつかったです。kinou wa totemo atsukatta desu.It was very hot yesterday.
きょうの テストは たいへん むずかしかったです。kyou no tesuto wa taihen muzukashikatta desu.Today's test was very difficult.

6.10 A little and not very: chotto and amari (bunkei 6.6)

Chotto means a little. Put it in front of an adjective, and the adjective keeps its normal form: chotto semai desu (it is a little small). Chotto also makes a refusal sound soft. Sumimasen, ima chotto isogashii desu is a polite way to say you cannot do something now.

Amari means not very, and it must always be followed by a negative ending. Say amari takakunai desu (not very expensive) or amari kantan ja arimasen (not very easy), and never amari takai desu. It works in the past as well: amari muzukashikunakatta desu (it was not very difficult).

To pick the right adverb, remember this: totemo, taihen and chotto go with positive endings, and amari goes only with negative endings.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
すみません、いま ちょっと いそがしいです。sumimasen, ima chotto isogashii desu.Sorry, I am a little busy now.
それは ちょっと ちいさいです。sore wa chotto chiisai desu.That is a little small.
このカメラは ちょっと ふるいです。kono kamera wa chotto furui desu.This camera is a little old.
わたしの へやは ちょっと せまいです。watashi no heya wa chotto semai desu.My room is a little small.
あした あまり ひまじゃありません。ashita amari hima ja arimasen.I am not very free tomorrow.
もんだいは あまり かんたんじゃありません。mondai wa amari kantan ja arimasen.The problem is not very easy.
えきは あまり とおくないです。eki wa amari tookunai desu.The station is not very far.
このえいがは あまり おもしろくないです。kono eiga wa amari omoshirokunai desu.This movie is not very interesting.
かんじの しけんは あまり むずかしくなかったです。kanji no shiken wa amari muzukashikunakatta desu.The kanji test was not very difficult.

6.11 Putting it together: sentences and questions with adjectives

This last lesson is an extra that pulls the chapter together, because the exercises mix everything. A full adjective sentence follows the pattern A wa (adverb) adjective desu. The adverb is optional, and the last word of the sentence carries the tense.

A yes or no question just adds ka, and you answer with hai or iie. In a no answer the adjective turns negative: iie, hima ja arimasen. You can also give the true answer after it, as in iie, atsukunakatta desu. samukatta desu (No, it was not hot. It was cold.).

To describe where something is, build the description in front of the noun and finish with ni arimasu or ga arimasu: ie no chikaku ni hirokute shizuka na kouen ga arimasu. When two adjectives describe one noun, the first one joins with kute or de, and the last one goes straight in front of the noun (with na if it needs it).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
このへやは ひろいです。kono heya wa hiroi desu.This room is wide.
このへやは とても ひろいです。kono heya wa totemo hiroi desu.This room is very wide.
このへやは あまり ひろくないです。kono heya wa amari hirokunai desu.This room is not very wide.
どようびは ひまですか。doyoubi wa hima desu ka.Are you free on Saturday?
はい、ひまです。hai, hima desu.Yes, I am free.
いいえ、ひまじゃありません。iie, hima ja arimasen.No, I am not free.
きのうは あつかったですか。kinou wa atsukatta desu ka.Was it hot yesterday?
いいえ、あつくなかったです。 さむかったです。iie, atsukunakatta desu. samukatta desu.No, it was not hot. It was cold.
このアパートは きれいで しずかな ところに あります。kono apa-to wa kirei de shizuka na tokoro ni arimasu.This apartment is in a clean, quiet place.
いえの ちかくに ひろくて しずかな こうえんが あります。ie no chikaku ni hirokute shizuka na kouen ga arimasu.There is a wide, quiet park near my house.
きょうしつの なかに ながい テーブルが あります。kyoushitsu no naka ni nagai te-buru ga arimasu.There is a long table in the classroom.
これは おおきくて おもい ほんです。kore wa ookikute omoi hon desu.This is a big, heavy book.
せんせいは あかるくて やさしい ひとです。sensei wa akarukute yasashii hito desu.The teacher is a bright, kind person.
きょうの テストは たいへん むずかしかったです。kyou no tesuto wa taihen muzukashikatta desu.Today's test was very difficult.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Kirei and yuumei end in i but are na-adjectives

  • kirei (clean, beautiful) and yuumei (famous) look like i-adjectives, but they are na-adjectives.
  • Say kirei na heya and yuumei na kouen, with na in front of a noun.
  • The negative is kirei ja arimasen, never kirekunai.
  • Look for the (na) mark in the vocabulary list whenever you learn a new adjective.

Na before a noun, but not before desu

  • kirei na heya (a clean room) needs na, because a noun follows.
  • heya wa kirei desu (the room is clean) has no na, because desu follows.
  • The same goes for shizuka, benri, kantan, nigiyaka, hima, fuben, rippa, iroiro and yuumei.

Past and negative of i-adjectives

  • The adjective changes, not desu: takakatta desu (was expensive), never takai deshita.
  • Negative: takakunai desu. Past negative: takakunakatta desu.
  • The word ii is the exception. It uses yoi, so you get yokunai, yokatta and yokunakatta.
  • A na-adjective works like a noun: desu becomes deshita, and ja arimasen gets deshita added.

Tsumaranai ends in nai but is not a negative

  • tsumaranai (boring) is a normal i-adjective that happens to end in nai.
  • Its negative is tsumaranakunai (not boring), and its past is tsumaranakatta.
  • The negative ending kunai is added to other adjectives, such as takakunai.

Ja arimasen and dewa arimasen

  • Both mean the same, and both are polite. ja is the short form of dewa.
  • The word dewa is written では, and the は is read wa.
  • Add deshita to either one for the past: ja arimasen deshita or dewa arimasen deshita.

Kute and de when joining adjectives

  • An i-adjective drops the final i and adds kute: akarukute hiroi.
  • A na-adjective adds de: kirei de yasashii.
  • The word ii becomes yokute: yokute yasui.
  • Only the last adjective carries the tense: akarukute hirokatta desu.

Amari needs a negative, totemo and chotto do not

  • amari takakunai desu (not very expensive) is right. amari takai desu is wrong.
  • totemo takai desu (very expensive) and chotto takai desu (a little expensive) keep the positive ending.
  • totemo and taihen both mean very, and they are used the same way.
  • With a na-adjective, amari takes ja arimasen: amari hima ja arimasen.

Dou and donna

  • dou asks how something is and stands on its own: nihongo no kurasu wa dou desu ka.
  • donna must be followed by a noun: donna hito desu ka.
  • Both are answered with adjectives. For donna, repeat the noun: yasashii hito desu.
  • For a past question, use deshita: dou deshita ka.

Takai has two meanings

  • takai means expensive (takai jitensha) or high, tall (takai tatemono).
  • The opposite tells you which one is meant: yasui for expensive, hikui for high.

Atsui has three meanings

  • atsui means hot for things (atsui ko-hi-), hot for weather (kyou wa atsui desu) or thick (atsui hon).
  • The opposites are tsumetai (cold things), samui (cold weather) and usui (thin).
  • In kanji the three atsui words are written differently, so kanji will separate them later.

Yasashii and kantan

  • yasashii (an i-adjective) can mean kind or easy, as in yasashii sensei (a kind teacher).
  • kantan (a na-adjective) means easy only, as in kantan na shiken (an easy exam).

Warui and mazui

  • warui means bad in general.
  • mazui only means bad taste, so it describes food and drink.
  • The opposite of mazui is oishii (delicious), and the opposite of warui is ii (good).

Omoshiroi and tanoshii

  • The two words are close, but the book uses them in different places.
  • tanoshii describes a party, a job and Japanese study.
  • omoshiroi describes a book and a movie, and it can also mean funny.

Tokoro, basho, tatemono and biru

  • tokoro and basho both mean place.
  • tatemono and biru both mean building. biru is the short form of the English word.
  • tesuto and shiken both mean test, and tesuto is the katakana word from English.

Ji, kanji and the ji in ichiji

  • ji (character, letter) is any written symbol, and kanji is specifically a Chinese character.
  • The ji in ichiji (one o'clock) is a different word that sounds the same.
  • jikan (time, hours) also uses that second ji.

Hanami, hanabi and the seasons

  • hanami (flower viewing) belongs to spring, and hanabi (fireworks) belongs to summer.
  • suzushii (cool) is the pleasant kind of cool, and the reading uses it for autumn.
  • atsui and samui describe the weather, while tsumetai describes things you touch.

#AnswerWhy
1i-adjectivetakai is an i-adjective. It changes its own ending: takakunai, takakatta.

3na-adjectiveIt needs na in front of a noun: shizuka na tokoro.

6i-adjectiveisogashii is an i-adjective: isogashikatta.
7na-adjectivebenri needs na in front of a noun: benri na mise.
8na-adjectivehima is a na-adjective: hima ja arimasen.
9i-adjectiveatarashii is an i-adjective: atarashii kamera.
10na-adjectivenigiyaka needs na in front of a noun: nigiyaka na tokoro.
11i-adjectivetsumaranai ends in nai, but it is an i-adjective: tsumaranakunai.
12na-adjectivekantan needs na in front of a noun: kantan na shiken.
13i-adjectiveabunai is an i-adjective: abunai michi.
14na-adjectiverippa needs na in front of a noun: rippa na tatemono.
15na-adjectiveiroiro needs na in front of a noun: iroiro na mondai.

8hai, muzukashii desu. (はい、むずかしいです。)Say hai with muzukashii desu. For no, say iie, amari muzukashikunai desu.
