title: Daily Routines
intro: Chapter 7 teaches you your first verbs, so you can talk about your daily routine. You learn the four formal verb endings (masu, masen, mashita, masen deshita) and the verbs for waking up, sleeping, working, studying and resting. Then you say when things happen with ni, kara, made, goro and de, describe how an action is done with adverbs made from i-adjectives and na-adjectives (hayaku okimasu, shizuka ni benkyoushimasu), and say how often with itsumo, tokidoki and zenzen.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
7.1 Verbs in the formal form (masu, masen, mashita, masen deshita)

This is the first chapter with verbs, which are the action words: wake up, sleep, work, study. The book uses the formal (polite) form for now. It is built from a verb stem plus an ending. The stem is what is left when you take masu (ます) off: ne for nemasu, oki for okimasu and hajimari for hajimarimasu.

Four endings give you four forms. Masu is the present positive, masen is the present negative, mashita is the past positive and masen deshita is the past negative. The book shows the pattern with nemasu: nemasu (sleep), nemasen (do not sleep), nemashita (slept) and nemasen deshita (did not sleep). Notice that the past negative is the only form with two words, masen plus deshita, just like ja arimasen deshita in Chapter 6.

Japanese has no separate future tense. The present form covers both now and later, so raigetsu owarimasu means it finishes next month. The time word in the sentence tells you which one is meant. Words such as benkyou (study), shigoto (work), zangyou (overtime) and kyuukei (break) become verbs when you add shimasu, and only the shimasu part changes: benkyoushimasen, benkyoushimashita, benkyoushimasen deshita.

Umaremasu (be born) is in the word list, but the workbook never uses it. Because being born has already happened, you will mostly meet it in the past: umaremashita. The dictionary form of verbs, the one you look up in a dictionary, comes later in Chapter 9, so for now you only need the masu forms.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ねますnemasusleep, will sleep (present positive)
ねませんnemasendo not sleep, will not sleep (present negative)
ねましたnemashitaslept (past positive)
ねませんでしたnemasen deshitadid not sleep (past negative)
おきますokimasuwake up, will wake up
おきませんokimasendo not wake up, will not wake up
おきましたokimashitawoke up
おきませんでしたokimasen deshitadid not wake up
しごとしますshigotoshimasuwork (shigoto plus shimasu)
しごとしませんshigotoshimasendo not work, will not work
しごとしましたshigotoshimashitaworked
しごとしませんでしたshigotoshimasen deshitadid not work
らいげつ おわります。raigetsu owarimasu.It finishes next month. (the present form is also the future)
きのう べんきょうしました。kinou benkyoushimashita.I studied yesterday.
わたしは ごがつに うまれました。watashi wa gogatsu ni umaremashita.I was born in May.

7.2 Time expression + ni + verb (bunkei 7.1)

The marker ni goes after a specific time and tells you when the action happens: at 5:30, on Saturday, in December. The pattern is time + ni + verb, and it works with all four verb forms.

Ni is used only with specific times: a clock time (goji han ni), a day of the week (doyoubi ni), a month (juunigatsu ni) or a date (tooka ni). Time words that are not specific take no ni. These are the relative words such as kinou, ashita, asatte, yuube, konban, mainichi, maiasa, kesa, konshuu, senshuu, raishuu, raigetsu and sensenshuu. You say raigetsu owarimasu, never raigetsu ni owarimasu.

Here is a quick test. If the time word could be the answer to nanji (what time), nanyoubi (what day of the week), nangatsu (what month) or nannichi (what day of the month), then it takes ni. Words like kinou and mainichi do not answer any of those, so they take no ni.

The rows below use the book's examples. The verb part of each sentence does not change when you add ni. Pay attention to which rows have a ni and which do not.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ごじはんに おきます。goji han ni okimasu.wake up at 5:30
どようびに やすみます。doyoubi ni yasumimasu.take a holiday on Saturday
まいにち ざんぎょうします。mainichi zangyoushimasu.work overtime every day (no ni)
らいげつ おわります。raigetsu owarimasu.finish next month (no ni)
くじはんに きゅうけいしません。kuji han ni kyuukeishimasen.will not take a break at 9:30
にちようびに やすみません。nichiyoubi ni yasumimasen.will not take a holiday on Sunday
あさって しごとしません。asatte shigotoshimasen.will not work the day after tomorrow (no ni)
こんばん べんきょうしません。konban benkyoushimasen.will not study tonight (no ni)
じゅういちじに ねました。juuichiji ni nemashita.slept at 11 o'clock
じゅうにがつに おわりました。juunigatsu ni owarimashita.finished in December
せんせんしゅう はじまりました。sensenshuu hajimarimashita.started the week before last (no ni)
きのう べんきょうしました。kinou benkyoushimashita.studied yesterday (no ni)
いちがつに おわりませんでした。ichigatsu ni owarimasen deshita.did not finish in January
ろくじに おきませんでした。rokuji ni okimasen deshita.did not wake up at 6 o'clock
せんしゅう はじまりませんでした。senshuu hajimarimasen deshita.did not start last week (no ni)
ゆうべ ねませんでした。yuube nemasen deshita.did not sleep last night (no ni)

7.3 Time expression + kara + verb (bunkei 7.2)

Kara means from, and it marks the time when something starts. You met kara in Chapter 4 in sentences like kuji kara desu. Now it goes in front of a verb: sanji kara kyuukeishimasu means take a break from 3 o'clock.

Kara goes straight after the time word, with no ni added. You say sanji kara, not sanji ni kara. It also works with relative words such as ashita and raigetsu, so ashita kara benkyoushimasu is study from tomorrow.

Kara and made are a natural pair, because together they give the start and the end of an action: kuji kara juuji made kyuukeishimasu. The next lesson looks at made.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
さんじから きゅうけいします。sanji kara kyuukeishimasu.take a break from 3 o'clock
らいげつから やすみます。raigetsu kara yasumimasu.take a holiday from next month
しちじから しごとしました。shichiji kara shigotoshimashita.worked from 7 o'clock
あしたから べんきょうします。ashita kara benkyoushimasu.study from tomorrow
にがつから はたらきません。nigatsu kara hatarakimasen.will not work from February
くじから じゅうじまで きゅうけいします。kuji kara juuji made kyuukeishimasu.take a break from 9 o'clock until 10 o'clock

7.4 Time expression + made + verb (bunkei 7.3)

Made means until, and it marks the time when something stops. Like kara, it goes straight after the time word with no ni: kuji han made kyuukeishimashita is took a break until 9:30.

Made works best with verbs that go on for a while, such as yasumimasu (rest), shigotoshimasu (work), benkyoushimasu (study) and kyuukeishimasu (take a break). That is why you do not see it with a one-moment verb like okimasu. It makes sense to rest until March, but it does not make much sense to wake up until March.

You can combine the two markers to say from when until when, as in getsuyoubi kara kinyoubi made shigotoshimasu (work from Monday until Friday). The same words kara and made worked with places in Chapter 5, so you are just reusing them with time.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ことしの さんがつまで やすみます。kotoshi no sangatsu made yasumimasu.will rest until March this year
くじはんまで きゅうけいしました。kuji han made kyuukeishimashita.took a break until 9:30
らいねんまで しごとします。rainen made shigotoshimasu.work until next year
よるまで べんきょうしました。yoru made benkyoushimashita.studied until night
よっかまで やすみます。yokka made yasumimasu.take a holiday until the 4th
げつようびから きんようびまで しごとします。getsuyoubi kara kinyoubi made shigotoshimasu.work from Monday until Friday

7.5 Time expression + goro + verb (bunkei 7.4)

Goro means around, and it gives a rough time. It goes right after the time word: shichiji han goro okimasu is wake up around 7:30. You first met goro in Chapter 4.

Goro is for a point in time, such as 7:30, next week, lunchtime or August. It is not for a length of time. For an amount of time you use gurai from Chapter 5: rokujikan gurai nemasu is sleep about 6 hours. A simple way to remember it is goro for the clock and gurai for the length.

The book writes goro without ni after it, so follow that for now: rokuji goro okimasu. If you are not sure which one to use, ask yourself whether the word names a moment (goro) or tells how long something lasts (gurai).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
しちじはんごろ おきます。shichiji han goro okimasu.wake up around 7:30
らいしゅうごろ はじまります。raishuu goro hajimarimasu.start around next week
じゅうにじはんごろ ねました。juuniji han goro nemashita.slept around 12:30
ひるごろ きゅうけいします。hiru goro kyuukeishimasu.take a break around lunchtime
はちがつごろ おわりました。hachigatsu goro owarimashita.finished around August
ろくじごろ おきます。rokuji goro okimasu.wake up around 6 o'clock
ろくじかんぐらい ねます。rokujikan gurai nemasu.sleep about 6 hours

7.6 Span of time + de + verb (bunkei 7.5)

This pattern uses a length of time, not a point on the clock. Span of time + de + verb says that the action will happen within that length of time: sanjuppun de owarimasu is finish within 30 minutes, and ichijikan de hajimarimasu is start within an hour. Think of de as showing how much time passes or is needed before the action.

The spans come from Chapter 5: sanjuppun (30 minutes), ichijikan (1 hour), juugofun (15 minutes) and ikkagetsu (1 month). Do not mix them up with clock times. Ichiji is one o'clock, but ichijikan is one hour.

Add ato in front to say after: ato juugofun de kyuukeishimasu is take a break after 15 minutes. The book marks ato with a star because it is extra. The sentence works without it, and ato just makes the meaning clearer.

Be careful with ni. A length of time with de does not take ni, so you say ichijikan de, never ichijikan ni de. Ni after a length of time is used for something else, how often, which is lesson 7.12.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
さんじゅっぷんで おわります。sanjuppun de owarimasu.finish within 30 minutes
いちじかんで はじまります。ichijikan de hajimarimasu.start within an hour
あと じゅうごふんで きゅうけいします。ato juugofun de kyuukeishimasu.take a break after 15 minutes
あと いっかげつで やすみます。ato ikkagetsu de yasumimasu.take a holiday after a month
あと さんじゅっぷんで ねます。ato sanjuppun de nemasu.sleep after 30 minutes
にほんごの クラスは いっかげつで おわります。nihongo no kurasu wa ikkagetsu de owarimasu.The Japanese class finishes within a month.

7.7 I-adjective as an adverb (bunkei 7.6)

An adjective can describe how an action is done. To use an i-adjective this way, drop the final i and add ku, then put it right before the verb. Hayai (early) becomes hayaku, so hayaku okimasu is wake up early. Osoi (late) becomes osoku, so osoku nemashita is slept late.

The word ii (good) does not change directly. As in Chapter 6, it borrows its other form yoi, so you get yoku: yoku nemashita is slept well. Hayai and osoi each have two meanings, early or fast and late or slow. In this chapter, with these verbs, they mean early and late.

Do not use kute here. In Chapter 6 you added kute to join two adjectives, as in akarukute hiroi. Before a verb you want plain ku, so hayaku okimasu is right and hayakute okimasu is wrong.

Notice that only the adjective changes. The verb keeps its own form, so you can use the same hayaku with okimasu, okimashita or okimasen.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
はやくhayakuearly (from hayai)
おそくosokulate (from osoi)
よくyokuwell (from ii, which uses yoi)
はやく おきます。hayaku okimasu.wake up early
おそく おわります。osoku owarimasu.finish late
はやく はじまりました。hayaku hajimarimashita.started early
おそく ねました。osoku nemashita.slept late
はやく おわります。hayaku owarimasu.finish early
おそく はじまりました。osoku hajimarimashita.started late
よく ねました。yoku nemashita.slept well

7.8 Na-adjective as an adverb (bunkei 7.7)

A na-adjective can also describe an action, but it changes in a different way. Drop the na and add ni, then put it in front of the verb. Shizuka na becomes shizuka ni, so shizuka ni kyuukeishimasu is take a break quietly. Majime na becomes majime ni, so majime ni benkyoushimashita is studied seriously.

That is the na in the (na) mark of the word lists: it is the part that is replaced. In front of a noun the na stays, as in shizuka na gakusei (a quiet student). In front of a verb it becomes ni, as in shizuka ni benkyoushimasu (study quietly).

Kirei and kantan from Chapter 6 are na-adjectives too, so they also take ni: kirei ni hatarakimasu and kantan ni owarimashita. Remember that the sound of the word does not decide the type. Kirei ends in i but still uses ni, not ku.

A quick way to choose: i-adjectives take ku and na-adjectives take ni. Lesson 7.13 puts both side by side.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
しずかにshizuka niquietly (from shizuka na)
まじめにmajime niseriously (from majime na)
げんきにgenki niin good health, well (from genki na)
きれいにkirei nicleanly, nicely (from kirei na)
かんたんにkantan nieasily (from kantan na)
しずかに きゅうけいします。shizuka ni kyuukeishimasu.take a break quietly
まじめに べんきょうしました。majime ni benkyoushimashita.studied seriously
げんきに おきました。genki ni okimashita.woke up well, in good health
きれいに はたらきます。kirei ni hatarakimasu.work cleanly
しずかに べんきょうしました。shizuka ni benkyoushimashita.studied quietly
かんたんに おわりました。kantan ni owarimashita.finished easily
まじめに しごとします。majime ni shigotoshimasu.work seriously

7.9 Tokidoki (bunkei 7.8)

Tokidoki means sometimes. You add it to a sentence to say that the action is done now and then. Hachiji ni okimasu is wake up at 8 o'clock, and tokidoki hachiji ni okimasu is sometimes wake up at 8 o'clock.

The book puts tokidoki at the start of the sentence, in front of the time and the other details. You do not change the verb or add any marker. In the third row, osoku made means until late, which is osoku (late) plus made (until).

Tokidoki is one of three how-often words in this chapter. The other two are itsumo (always, next lesson) and zenzen (never, lesson 7.11).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ときどき はちじに おきます。tokidoki hachiji ni okimasu.sometimes wake up at 8 o'clock
ときどき にちようびに しごとします。tokidoki nichiyoubi ni shigotoshimasu.sometimes work on Sunday
ときどき おそくまで はたらきます。tokidoki osoku made hatarakimasu.sometimes work until late
ときどき あさはやく べんきょうします。tokidoki asa hayaku benkyoushimasu.sometimes study early in the morning
ときどき おそく ねます。tokidoki osoku nemasu.sometimes sleep late

7.10 Itsumo (bunkei 7.9)

Itsumo means always. Like tokidoki, it goes at the start of the sentence and does not change the verb: rokuji ni okimasu is wake up at 6 o'clock, and itsumo rokuji ni okimasu is always wake up at 6 o'clock.

The sentence does not have to be positive. Itsumo zangyoushimasen means always do not work overtime, which comes out as never work overtime. Be careful, because zenzen (next lesson) can give a very similar meaning. Itsumo with a negative says it is always not done, while zenzen says it is not done at all.

Kurisumasu wa yasumimasu in the third row uses wa to mark Christmas as the topic, and it means take Christmas off. Christmas is not a time like 6 o'clock, so the sentence has no ni.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
いつも ろくじに おきます。itsumo rokuji ni okimasu.always wake up at 6 o'clock
いつも くじに きゅうけいします。itsumo kuji ni kyuukeishimasu.always take a break at 9 o'clock
いつも クリスマスは やすみます。itsumo kurisumasu wa yasumimasu.always take Christmas off
いつも おそく ねます。itsumo osoku nemasu.always sleep late
いつも ざんぎょうしません。itsumo zangyoushimasen.never work overtime (always not)

7.11 Zenzen + negative (bunkei 7.10)

Zenzen means never or not at all, and it always needs a negative ending. Goji han ni okimasen is do not wake up at 5:30, and goji han ni zenzen okimasen is never wake up at 5:30.

Put zenzen right before the verb or the adverb that goes with it. When the sentence has a time word, zenzen comes after it: goji han ni zenzen okimasen. When there is no time word, it can start the sentence: zenzen osoku nemasen.

Zenzen works in the past too, with masen deshita: kinou zenzen benkyoushimasen deshita is did not study at all yesterday. You cannot use it with a positive verb, so zenzen okimasu is wrong.

This works just like amari from Chapter 6. Both need a negative ending, but they say different things. Amari means not very, a little bit true, while zenzen means not at all, not true in any way.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ごじはんに ぜんぜん おきません。goji han ni zenzen okimasen.never wake up at 5:30
まいにち ぜんぜん べんきょうしません。mainichi zenzen benkyoushimasen.do not study at all on any day
にちようびに ぜんぜん しごとしません。nichiyoubi ni zenzen shigotoshimasen.never work on Sunday
ぜんぜん おそく ねません。zenzen osoku nemasen.never sleep late
ぜんぜん はやく おわりません。zenzen hayaku owarimasen.never finish early
せんしゅう ぜんぜん はたらきませんでした。senshuu zenzen hatarakimasen deshita.did not work at all last week
きのう ぜんぜん べんきょうしませんでした。kinou zenzen benkyoushimasen deshita.did not study at all yesterday

7.12 Asking about time and how often (extra lesson)

The exercises keep asking questions about time, so here is a map of the question words. Nanji ni asks at what time, and you answer with a clock time plus ni: rokuji ni okimasu. Nanji goro asks around what time, and you answer with goro: rokuji goro okimasu. Itsu asks when, and it takes no ni: nihongo no kurasu wa itsu hajimarimasu ka.

Nanjikan asks for a length of time, how many hours. You answer with a length such as rokujikan or nanajikan, and gurai makes it about: nanjikan gurai benkyoushimasu ka. Do not confuse it with nanji, which is a clock time. A good test is that nanji goes with ni and goro, and nanjikan goes with gurai and de.

To say how often, use a length of time plus ni, then the number of times: isshuukan ni nikai yasumimasu is rest twice a week. Ask it with nankai (how many times). You learned this pattern in Chapter 5, and the counts are ikkai (once), nikai (twice), sankai (three times) and so on.

Finally, donogurai from Chapter 5 asks how long something takes, and you answer with a length and kakarimasu: firipin kara nihon made hikouki de yojikan gurai kakarimasu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
なんじに おきますか。nanji ni okimasu ka.What time do you wake up?
まいあさ なんじごろ おきますか。maiasa nanji goro okimasu ka.Around what time do you wake up every morning?
けさ なんじに おきましたか。kesa nanji ni okimashita ka.What time did you wake up this morning?
にほんごの クラスは いつ はじまりましたか。nihongo no kurasu wa itsu hajimarimashita ka.When did the Japanese class start?
にほんごの クラスは いつ おわりますか。nihongo no kurasu wa itsu owarimasu ka.When does the Japanese class finish?
まいばん なんじかん ねますか。maiban nanjikan nemasu ka.How many hours do you sleep every night?
まいしゅう なんじかんぐらい べんきょうしますか。maishuu nanjikan gurai benkyoushimasu ka.About how many hours do you study every week?
いっしゅうかんに なんかい やすみますか。isshuukan ni nankai yasumimasu ka.How many times a week do you rest?
いっしゅうかんに いっかい やすみます。isshuukan ni ikkai yasumimasu.I rest once a week.

フィリピンから にほんまで どのぐらい かかりますか。firipin kara nihon made donogurai kakarimasu ka.How long does it take from the Philippines to Japan?

7.13 Putting it together: word order and tense (extra lesson)

This last lesson pulls the chapter together, because the exercises mix everything. A sentence with a verb usually follows this order: the topic with wa, the time (with ni if it is a specific time), a how-often word or adverb, and the verb at the very end. For example, maiasa rokuji goro hayaku okimasu has a time word, a goro time, an adverb and then the verb.

The verb always comes last, and it carries the tense. Match the tense to the time word. Kinou, yuube, kesa, ototoi, senshuu and sengetsu are in the past, so use mashita or masen deshita. Ashita, asatte, konban, konshuu, raishuu and raigetsu are in the future, so use masu or masen. Mainichi, maiasa and maiban describe habits, so they use masu or masen too.

When an adjective describes the verb, an i-adjective drops its i and takes ku, and a na-adjective takes ni: hayaku okimasu and majime ni benkyoushimasu. A na-adjective in front of a noun keeps na instead: majime na gakusei. So for a na-adjective, na goes before a noun and ni goes before a verb.

Finally, the negative words zenzen and amari need a negative verb, while itsumo and tokidoki can go with positive or negative verbs. When you write an answer, check four things in order: the marker (ni or none), the adverb ending (ku or ni), the how-often word, and the verb tense.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Ni or no ni

  • A specific time takes ni: goji han ni, doyoubi ni, juunigatsu ni, tooka ni.
  • Relative time words take no ni: kinou, ashita, asatte, yuube, konban, mainichi, maiasa, kesa, konshuu, senshuu, raishuu and raigetsu.
  • Quick test: if the word could answer nanji, nanyoubi, nangatsu or nannichi, use ni.
  • The words kara, made and goro sit straight after the time, so you do not add ni: sanji kara, kuji han made, rokuji goro.

Goro or gurai

  • goro is around a point in time: rokuji goro (around 6 o'clock), raishuu goro (around next week).
  • gurai is about a length of time: rokujikan gurai (about 6 hours).
  • Ask yourself whether the word names a moment or tells how long. A moment takes goro and a length takes gurai.

Ji or jikan

  • ji is a clock time: rokuji is 6 o'clock, and nanji asks what time.
  • jikan is a length of time: rokujikan is 6 hours, and nanjikan asks how many hours.
  • rokuji ni nemasu means sleep at 6. rokujikan nemasu means sleep for 6 hours.
  • A clock time takes ni. A length of time takes no ni, except in the how-often pattern: isshuukan ni nikai.

Kara, made and de

  • kara is the start and made is the end: kuji kara juuji made.
  • de after a length of time means within it: ichijikan de owarimasu.
  • Do not use de with a clock time. juuji de does not mean until 10 o'clock, because made does that.
  • Put ato in front for after: ato juugofun de kyuukeishimasu.

Ku, ni and na

  • An i-adjective takes ku before a verb: hayaku okimasu.
  • A na-adjective takes ni before a verb: shizuka ni benkyoushimasu.
  • A na-adjective takes na before a noun: shizuka na gakusei.
  • kirei ends in i but it is a na-adjective, so say kirei ni, never kireku.

Ku, not kute, before a verb

  • kute joins two adjectives, as in akarukute hiroi.
  • Before a verb, use plain ku: hayaku okimasu. Hayakute okimasu is wrong.
  • The same split works for na-adjectives: de joins two adjectives, and ni goes before a verb.

Hayai and osoi have two meanings

  • hayai means early or fast, and osoi means late or slow.
  • With okimasu, nemasu and hajimarimasu they mean early and late.
  • The adverb forms are hayaku and osoku.
  • ii (good) uses yoi, so its adverb form is yoku, as in yoku nemashita.

Masen or masen deshita

  • masen is present or future, and masen deshita is past.
  • The time word decides. kinou, yuube, kesa, ototoi and senshuu are past.
  • kinou zenzen benkyoushimasen is wrong. Say kinou zenzen benkyoushimasen deshita.
  • ashita, konban, raishuu and raigetsu are future, so use masu or masen.

Zenzen and amari

  • Both need a negative ending.
  • zenzen means not at all: zenzen benkyoushimasen is do not study at all.
  • amari means not very: amari benkyoushimasen is do not study very much.
  • amari is from Chapter 6. zenzen is the stronger of the two.

Itsumo, tokidoki and zenzen

  • itsumo is always, tokidoki is sometimes and zenzen is never.
  • All three go at the start of the sentence or right before the verb: itsumo rokuji ni okimasu.
  • zenzen must have a negative verb. itsumo and tokidoki can go with either kind.

Hatarakimasu and shigotoshimasu

  • hatarakimasu and shigotoshimasu both mean work.
  • shigotoshimasu is just shigoto (work) plus shimasu.
  • The same trick works with benkyou, zangyou and kyuukei.
  • Only the shimasu part changes: benkyoushimasen, benkyoushimashita.

Yasumimasu, nemasu and yasumi

  • yasumimasu means rest or take a day off, and nemasu means sleep.
  • yasumi (a noun) is a holiday or a rest day, and hiruyasumi is a lunch break.
  • kyuukeishimasu is a short break during the day.
  • nemui (sleepy) shares its root with nemasu (sleep).

Verbs that look alike

  • hajimarimasu (start) and hatarakimasu (work) both begin with ha.
  • okimasu (wake up) and owarimasu (finish) both begin with o.
  • okimasu and nemasu are opposites, and so are hajimarimasu and owarimasu.

Nanji, nanjikan, nankai and itsu

  • nanji asks what time, and you answer with ni: rokuji ni.
  • nanjikan asks how many hours: rokujikan.
  • nankai asks how many times: nikai.
  • itsu asks when, and it takes no ni.

Nikai twice and nikai second floor

  • nikai can mean twice (2 times) or the second floor.
  • The sentence tells you which one: isshuukan ni nikai yasumimasu is rest twice a week.
  • kanji will separate them later, because twice is written with the kanji for times and second floor with the kanji for floor.

Ikkagetsu and hitotsuki

  • ikkagetsu and hitotsuki both mean one month.
  • This chapter uses ikkagetsu: ikkagetsu de owarimasu.

How strong is it?

  • From weakest to strongest: zenzen (not at all), amari (not very), chotto (a little), totemo (very) and taihen (very).
  • zenzen and amari need a negative ending. chotto, totemo and taihen go with a positive one.
  • The how-often words work the same way: itsumo (always) and tokidoki (sometimes) take a positive ending, and zenzen takes a negative one.

Part A: What does the word mean?

#AnswerWhy
1wake upokimasu is wake up. Its opposite is nemasu.
2starthajimarimasu is start. Its opposite is owarimasu.
3finishowarimasu is finish. Its opposite is hajimarimasu.
4work overtimezangyou (overtime) plus shimasu.
5take a breakkyuukei (break) plus shimasu.
6be bornYou will mostly see it in the past: umaremashita.
7doctorisha is a doctor.
8new employeeShinnyuu means new entry and shain is employee.
9strictkibishii is an i-adjective.
10sleepynemui shares its root with nemasu (sleep).
11serious, industriousmajime is a na-adjective: majime na gakusei.
12fine, healthygenki is a na-adjective: genki na gakusei.
13sometimestokidoki is one of the three how-often words.
14never, not at allzenzen always needs a negative ending.
15lunch breakhiru (noon) plus yasumi (rest).
16medicinekusuri is medicine. kusuriya (Chapter 6) is a drugstore.
17present, giftpurezento is a katakana word from English.
18credit cardkurejitto ka-do is a katakana word from English.

1okimasu (おきます)okimasu is wake up.
2nemasu (ねます)nemasu is sleep.

4hajimarimasu (はじまります)hajimarimasu is start.
5owarimasu (おわります)owarimasu is finish.

8benkyoushimasu (べんきょうします)benkyoushimasu is benkyou plus shimasu.

11tokidoki (ときどき)tokidoki is sometimes.
12hayai (はやい)hayai means early or fast.
13osoi (おそい)osoi means late or slow.

Part D: Verb forms

#AnswerWhy
1nemasen (ねません)Drop masu and add masen.
2okimashita (おきました)Drop masu and add mashita.
3hajimarimasen deshita (はじまりませんでした)Drop masu and add masen deshita.
4owarimasen (おわりません)Drop masu and add masen.
5hatarakimashita (はたらきました)Drop masu and add mashita.
6shigotoshimasen deshita (しごとしませんでした)Only the shimasu part changes: shimasen deshita.
7zangyoushimasen (ざんぎょうしません)Only the shimasu part changes: shimasen.
8benkyoushimashita (べんきょうしました)Only the shimasu part changes: shimashita.
9kyuukeishimasen deshita (きゅうけいしませんでした)Only the shimasu part changes: shimasen deshita.
10yasumimasen (やすみません)Drop masu and add masen.
11umaremashita (うまれました)Drop masu and add mashita.
12okimasu (おきます)The stem is oki. Add masu for the present.
13nemashita (ねました)The stem is ne. Add mashita for the past positive.
14hajimarimasen deshita (はじまりませんでした)Add deshita after masen to make the past negative.
15benkyoushimasen (べんきょうしません)The shimashita part becomes shimasen.
16zangyoushimasu (ざんぎょうします)The shimasen deshita part becomes shimasu.

10gogatsu futsuka ni hajimarimasen deshita. (ごがつふつかに はじまりませんでした。)The sentence is already past, so the negative is masen deshita. Meaning: It did not start on May 2nd.

Positive verbs end in mashita. Items 4 and 8 are negative, so they become masen deshita.

#AnswerWhy

A clock time or a day of the week takes ni. Relative words like ashita, yuube and mainichi do not. Item 5 is a goro or gurai choice, and goro is for a time of day.

title: Food, Drinks and Everyday Verbs
intro: Chapter 8 teaches you what you do to things: eat, drink, read, write, buy, sell, sing and call. You learn the new food, drink and reading words and 13 everyday verbs, then the small markers that say who and what and where. O marks the thing you act on, de marks the place, the method or the tool, ni marks who receives the action, and to marks who does it with you. You also learn the question words that go with each marker (nani o, doko de, dare ni, dare to, nani de, douyatte) and some handy phrases from short conversations.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
8.1 Transitive verbs and the verb list

Chapter 7 gave you verbs that stand on their own, like okimasu (wake up) and nemasu (sleep). Chapter 8 adds verbs that do something to something else, such as eat bread, read a book or write an email. These are called transitive verbs, and the thing the verb acts on is called the object. In Japanese the verb always comes last, and a small marker after each word tells you the job of that word. The next lessons go through those markers one by one.

All the verbs in this chapter are in the formal masu form from Chapter 7, so they have the same four endings: masu, masen, mashita and masen deshita. Take tabemasu (eat) as the model. Tabemasen is do not eat, tabemashita is ate and tabemasen deshita is did not eat. The stem is what is left when you drop masu, so tabe, nomi and yomi are the stems of tabemasu, nomimasu and yomimasu. The present form also covers the future, so tabemasu can mean eat or will eat.

The chapter has 13 verbs, and they are listed below. The dictionary form, the one you look up in a dictionary, comes later in Chapter 9, so for now you only need the masu forms.

Four of the verbs have more than one meaning. Kikimasu is listen or ask, hanashimasu is speak or talk, mimasu is watch, look or see, and oshiemasu is teach or tell. The markers around the verb tell you which meaning is meant. Kakemasu is almost always used in the set phrase denwa o kakemasu, which means make a phone call.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
たべますtabemasueat, will eat (present positive)
たべませんtabemasendo not eat, will not eat (present negative)
たべましたtabemashitaate (past positive)
たべませんでしたtabemasen deshitadid not eat (past negative)
のみますnomimasudrink
よみますyomimasuread
かきますkakimasuwrite
ききますkikimasulisten, ask
はなしますhanashimasuspeak, talk
みますmimasuwatch, look, see
かいますkaimasubuy
うりますurimasusell
おしえますoshiemasuteach, tell
うたいますutaimasusing
すいますsuimasusmoke
でんわを かけますdenwa o kakemasucall (make a phone call)
のみませんでしたnomimasen deshitadid not drink
よみましたyomimashitaread (past)

8.2 A wa object o transitive verb (bunkei 8.1)

The basic pattern is A wa object o verb. Wa marks the topic, who does the action. O marks the object, the thing the action is done to. The verb comes last and shows the tense and whether it is positive or negative. So ana san wa tokei o kaimasu is Ana will buy a watch. In kana the object marker is written を, but you say it just like the vowel o. A good habit is to ask what the action is done to, and then put o straight after that word.

The topic can be left out when everyone knows who is doing the action. Tokei o kaimasu on its own is fine, and it means I will buy a watch if you are the one talking. Remember that the present form also covers the future.

The book adds a note about negative sentences. When the verb is negative, the object marker o can change into wa to put the spotlight on that thing, for emphasis. Bi-ru o nomimasu is I drink beer, and wain wa nomimasen says that wine is the thing I do not drink. Wa is natural when you are comparing two things. You can also keep o in a negative sentence, as in the book's own example shousetsu o yomimasen, and that is fine too.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんは とけいを かいます。ana san wa tokei o kaimasu.Ana will buy a watch.
ジョンさんは ほんを よみます。jon san wa hon o yomimasu.John reads a book.
かちょうは メールを かきます。kachou wa me-ru o kakimasu.The section chief writes an email.
あには コーヒーを のみました。ani wa ko-hi- o nomimashita.My older brother drank coffee.
わたしは えいごを おしえました。watashi wa eigo o oshiemashita.I taught English.
おとうとは おんがくを ききます。otouto wa ongaku o kikimasu.My younger brother listens to music.
わたしは しょうせつを よみません。watashi wa shousetsu o yomimasen.I do not read novels.
キムさんは でんわを かけませんでした。kim san wa denwa o kakemasen deshita.Kim did not make a phone call.
ビールを のみます。bi-ru o nomimasu.I drink beer.
ワインは のみません。wain wa nomimasen.I do not drink wine (but I drink other things).
ぎゅうにゅうは のみません。gyuunyuu wa nomimasen.I do not drink milk (but I drink other things).

8.3 Time expression ni, kara, made or goro + transitive verb (bunkei 8.2)

The time words from Chapter 7 slot in before the object, so the pattern is time + object o + verb. The markers are the ones you already know: ni (at), kara (from), made (until) and goro (around). Maiasa asagohan o tabemasu is I eat breakfast every morning, and itou sensei wa sanji kara oshiemasu is Mr. Ito teaches from 3 o'clock.

The book has a note here. Ni is only for a specific time, such as a clock time, a day of the week, a month or a date. It is not used with non-specific time words like maiasa, maiban, mainichi, maishuu, kesa and kinou. Look at the rows to see the difference: nichiyoubi ni atarashii kutsu o kaimashita has ni, while kesa gyuunyuu o nomimashita does not. Kara, made and goro sit straight after the time word and never take ni.

The time word also helps you choose the tense. Kesa (this morning) and kinou (yesterday) are already past, so the verb ends in mashita.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
まいあさ あさごはんを たべます。maiasa asagohan o tabemasu.I eat breakfast every morning.
いとうせんせいは さんじから おしえます。itou sensei wa sanji kara oshiemasu.Mr. Ito teaches from 3 o'clock.
よる はちじごろ ニュースを みます。yoru hachiji goro nyu-su o mimasu.I watch the news at around 8 in the evening.
まいしゅう かいしゃの レポートを かきます。maishuu kaisha no repo-to o kakimasu.I write the company report every week.
にちようびに あたらしい くつを かいました。nichiyoubi ni atarashii kutsu o kaimashita.I bought new shoes on Sunday.
けさ ぎゅうにゅうを のみました。kesa gyuunyuu o nomimashita.I drank milk this morning.
まいばん しょうせつを よみます。maiban shousetsu o yomimasu.I read novels every night.
きんようびまで くすりを のみます。kinyoubi made kusuri o nomimasu.I will take medicine until Friday.
まいにち コーヒーを のみます。mainichi ko-hi- o nomimasu.I drink coffee every day.
じゅうにじはんに ひるごはんを たべました。juuniji han ni hirugohan o tabemashita.I ate lunch at 12:30.

8.4 Place of action de (bunkei 8.3)

De marks the place where an action happens or will happen, in English at or in. The pattern is place + de + (object o) + verb. Kissaten de ko-hi- o nomimasu is I drink coffee at the coffee shop. The question word is doko de, which means where.

Do not mix de up with ni from Chapter 5. Ni goes with imasu and arimasu to say where a person or a thing is. De goes with an action verb like nomimasu, tabemasu or benkyoushimasu to say where something happens. Compare the last two rows: kaisha de hatarakimasu is work at the company, and kaisha ni imasu is be at the company.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
きっさてんで コーヒーを のみます。kissaten de ko-hi- o nomimasu.I drink coffee at the coffee shop.
としょかんで べんきょうしました。toshokan de benkyoushimashita.I studied at the library.
だいがくで おしえます。daigaku de oshiemasu.I teach at the university.
カラオケで うたいました。karaoke de utaimashita.I sang at karaoke.
しょくどうで たべます。shokudou de tabemasu.I eat at the cafeteria.
えいがかんで えいがを みました。eigakan de eiga o mimashita.I watched a movie at the movie theater.
デパートで かいました。depa-to de kaimashita.I bought it at the department store.
にほんで はたらきます。nihon de hatarakimasu.I work in Japan.
かいしゃで はたらきます。kaisha de hatarakimasu.I work at the company.
かいしゃに います。kaisha ni imasu.I am at the company.

8.5 Recipient of action ni (bunkei 8.4)

Ni marks the person who receives the action, in English to or for. The pattern is person + ni + (object o) + verb. Ana san ni denwa o kakemasu is I will call Ana. The English word changes with the verb. You call to Ana, write to Mr. Tanaka and buy something for your brother, but Japanese uses the same ni each time. English also drops the little word in ask the teacher, and Japanese still says sensei ni kikimashita.

Notice what this does to kikimasu. With o after a thing, as in ongaku o kikimasu, it means listen. With ni after a person, as in sensei ni kikimasu, it means ask. The question words for a recipient are dare ni and the more polite donata ni.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんに でんわを かけます。ana san ni denwa o kakemasu.I will call Ana.
たなかさんに てがみを かきました。tanaka san ni tegami o kakimashita.I wrote a letter to Mr. Tanaka.
せんせいに ききました。sensei ni kikimashita.I asked the teacher.
あにに とけいを かいます。ani ni tokei o kaimasu.I will buy a watch for my older brother.
おかあさんに はなしました。okaasan ni hanashimashita.I spoke to my mother.
こどもに ほんを よみます。kodomo ni hon o yomimasu.I read books to the children.

8.6 Companion to or to issho ni (bunkei 8.5)

To marks the person who does the action together with you, in English with. The pattern is person + to + (object o) + verb. Shachou to hanashimashita is I spoke with the company president. You can add issho ni to stress the word together, as in ane to issho ni eiga o mimashita. The question words are dare to and the more polite donata to.

Ni or to? Ask yourself whether the other person joins in. If they do the action with you, use to. If they only receive the action, use ni. Tomodachi to ongaku o kikimasu is listen to music with a friend, but tomodachi ni denwa o kakemasu is call a friend. With hanashimasu both can work: shachou to hanashimashita is spoke with the president, and okaasan ni hanashimashita is spoke to my mother.

The same word to also joins two nouns and then it means and, as in pan to kudamono (bread and fruit). After a person and right before the verb it means with. The book's English for the Kim row says cellphone, but ko-ra is cola, so I wrote cola.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
しゃちょうと はなしました。shachou to hanashimashita.I spoke with the company president.
ともだちと おんがくを ききます。tomodachi to ongaku o kikimasu.I listen to music with friends.
あねといっしょに えいがを みました。ane to issho ni eiga o mimashita.I watched a movie with my older sister.
かぞくと ばんごはんを たべました。kazoku to bangohan o tabemashita.I ate dinner with my family.
キムさんと コーラを かいます。kim san to ko-ra o kaimasu.I will buy cola with Kim.
ベンさんと コーヒーを のみます。ben san to ko-hi- o nomimasu.I will drink coffee with Ben.
ともだちに でんわを かけます。tomodachi ni denwa o kakemasu.I will call a friend.
パンと くだものです。pan to kudamono desu.It is bread and fruit.

8.7 Method of action de (bunkei 8.6)

De also marks the method, which means how you do the action. Language words belong here, so nihongo de repo-to o kakimashita is I wrote the report in Japanese. The same goes for eigo de oshiemasu (teach in English) and kankokugo de hanashimashita (spoke in Korean).

De also works with other ways of doing things, such as denwa de (by phone) or terebi de (on TV). The question words are douyatte, which means how, and nani de. Do not add anything to the noun before de, so you say eigo de, not eigo no de.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ともだちと かんこくごで はなしました。tomodachi to kankokugo de hanashimashita.I spoke with my friends in Korean.
がくせいに えいごで おしえます。gakusei ni eigo de oshiemasu.I teach the students in English.
にほんごで レポートを かきました。nihongo de repo-to o kakimashita.I wrote the report in Japanese.
でんわで はなします。denwa de hanashimasu.I talk by phone.
テレビで ニュースを みます。terebi de nyu-su o mimasu.I watch the news on TV.

8.8 Tool of action de (bunkei 8.7)

When de marks a tool, it is the thing you use to do the action, in English with or using. Hashi de ra-men o tabemasu is I eat ramen with chopsticks. The tool comes before the object, and the object keeps its o.

Method and tool both use the same word de, so the sentences look alike. The noun tells you which one it is. A language, a phone or a TV is a method. Something you hold in your hand, like hashi, enpitsu or supu-n, is a tool. De therefore has three jobs in this chapter: place (doko de), method (douyatte or nani de) and tool (nani de). A quick test is to ask the question. Where does it happen? That is place. How do you do it? That is method. What do you use? That is tool.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
はしで ラーメンを たべます。hashi de ra-men o tabemasu.I eat ramen with chopsticks.
えんぴつで てがみを かきます。enpitsu de tegami o kakimasu.I write letters with a pencil.
スプーンで スープを のみます。supu-n de su-pu o nomimasu.I drink soup with a spoon.
フォークで ラーメンを たべます。fo-ku de ra-men o tabemasu.I eat ramen with a fork.
ボールペンで レポートを かきます。bo-rupen de repo-to o kakimasu.I write the report with a ballpoint pen.

8.9 Markers at a glance, and more sample sentences

The first six rows put every marker of the chapter in one place. After that come the book's nine sample sentences, which mix several markers in one sentence.

When a sentence has many parts, a common order is topic, time, companion, place, object and then the verb. The verb stays last, and the other parts can move around a little as long as each keeps its marker. Try to spot each marker and say what job it does.

Two patterns hide in the samples. A length of time, such as ichinenkan or juugofun, takes no marker at all. And isshuukan ni ikkai uses ni to mean per, so it reads once per week. You met that how-often pattern in Chapter 5.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
をomarks the object, what the action is done to
でdemarks the place of action: at, in
にnimarks the recipient: to, for
とtomarks the companion: with
でdemarks the method: in, by
でdemarks the tool: with, using
らいしゅうの にちようびに ともだちと えいがを みます。raishuu no nichiyoubi ni tomodachi to eiga o mimasu.I will watch a movie with a friend next Sunday.
ゆうべ ははに でんわを かけました。yuube haha ni denwa o kakemashita.I called my mother last night.
いっしゅうかんに いっかい かいしゃの レポートを かきます。isshuukan ni ikkai kaisha no repo-to o kakimasu.I write the company report once a week.
せんせいと きょうしつで じゅうごふん はなしました。sensei to kyoushitsu de juugofun hanashimashita.I talked with the teacher in the classroom for 15 minutes.
まいにち かぞくと ばんごはんを たべます。mainichi kazoku to bangohan o tabemasu.I eat dinner with my family every day.
にほんで いちねんかん べんきょうしました。nihon de ichinenkan benkyoushimashita.I studied in Japan for one year.
やまださんは モールで あたらしい カメラを かいました。yamada san wa mo-ru de atarashii kamera o kaimashita.Mr. Yamada bought a new camera at the mall.
せんせいは にほんごで おしえます。sensei wa nihongo de oshiemasu.The teacher teaches in Japanese.
おとうとは いつも へやで おんがくを ききます。otouto wa itsumo heya de ongaku o kikimasu.My younger brother always listens to music in his room.

8.10 Question words with the markers

A question word replaces the part you want to know, and it keeps the same marker its answer will take. If the answer takes o, the question is nani o. If the answer takes de for a place, the question is doko de. Swap the question word for the real answer and the marker stays where it is.

Dare means who, and donata is the polite version. Nani de and douyatte both ask how, and nani de also asks what tool. You ask a tool question with nani de and a language question with douyatte or nani de. The book lists these question words in a table, and then gives seven pairs of a question and its answer. The first six rows are the table, and the pairs follow.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
なにをnani owhat (object)
どこでdoko dewhere (place)
だれに / どなたにdare ni / donata nito or for whom (recipient)
だれと / どなたとdare to / donata towith whom (companion)
なにで / どうやってnani de / douyattehow (method)
なにでnani dewith what tool, or how (tool)
けさ なにを たべましたか。kesa nani o tabemashita ka.What did you eat this morning?
けさ パンを たべました。kesa pan o tabemashita.I ate bread this morning.
だれに メールを かきましたか。dare ni me-ru o kakimashita ka.Who did you write the email to?
かちょうに メールを かきました。kachou ni me-ru o kakimashita.I wrote the email to the section chief.
ラーメンを なにで たべますか。ra-men o nani de tabemasu ka.What do you eat ramen with?
はしで たべます。hashi de tabemasu.I eat it with chopsticks.
それを どこで かいましたか。sore o doko de kaimashita ka.Where did you buy that?
ほんやで かいました。honya de kaimashita.I bought it at the bookstore.
だれと えいがを みますか。dare to eiga o mimasu ka.Who will you watch a movie with?
アナさんと えいがを みます。ana san to eiga o mimasu.I will watch a movie with Ana.
どうやって おしえますか。douyatte oshiemasu ka.How do you teach?
えいごで おしえます。eigo de oshiemasu.I teach in English.
なにを よみますか。nani o yomimasu ka.What do you read?
しょうせつを よみます。shousetsu o yomimasu.I read novels.

8.11 Phrases from the conversations

The five short conversations on page 124 give you real-life lines that use the patterns of this chapter. Each row below is one line, and the English column shows who says it: Ana and Mari in the first, second and last conversations, and Kim and Ben in the other two.

A few small words are worth knowing. Jouzu means good at, and nihongo ga jouzu desu ne is a compliment. A modest reply is iie, madamada desu, which means no, not yet. Donogurai asks how long, and ikura gurai asks about how much. Dou deshita ka asks how something was. The little word yo at the end of a sentence adds a friendly you know, and ne asks for agreement, as in sou desu ne. Chotto before muzukashii makes it a little difficult.

Look for the markers as you read. Doko de nihongo o benkyoushimashita ka has doko de for the place and o for the object, and pan to kudamono desu uses to to mean and. In the second conversation the book notes that nihongo ga jouzu desu means good at Nihongo, and madamada means not yet.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
まいにち レポートを かきますか。mainichi repo-to o kakimasu ka.Ana: Do you write a report every day?
はい、まいにち レポートを かきます。hai, mainichi repo-to o kakimasu.Mari: Yes, I write a report every day.
えいごの レポートですか。eigo no repo-to desu ka.Ana: Is it a report in English?

にほんごが じょうずですね。nihongo ga jouzu desu ne.Ana: You are good at Japanese.
いいえ、まだまだです。iie, madamada desu.Mari: No, not yet.

にほんごの がっこうで べんきょうしました。nihongo no gakkou de benkyoushimashita.Mari: I studied at a Japanese language school.
どのぐらいですか。donogurai desu ka.Ana: About how long?
じゅっかげつぐらいです。jukkagetsu gurai desu.Mari: About 10 months.
にほんごの べんきょうは どうでしたか。nihongo no benkyou wa dou deshita ka.Ana: How was your Japanese study?
おもしろかったです。omoshirokatta desu.Mari: It was interesting.
ゆうべ なんじごろ ねましたか。yuube nanji goro nemashita ka.Kim: About what time did you go to bed last night?
ゆうべは じゅうじごろでした。yuube wa juuji goro deshita.Ben: It was around 10 last night.
べんきょうしましたか。benkyoushimashita ka.Kim: Did you study?
いいえ、ほんを よみました。キムさんは？iie, hon o yomimashita. kim san wa?Ben: No, I read a book. How about you, Kim?
わたしは ゆうべ はやく ねましたよ。watashi wa yuube hayaku nemashita yo.Kim: I went to bed early last night.
なんじごろですか。nanji goro desu ka.Ben: About what time?
くじごろです。kuji goro desu.Kim: Around 9.
きょねん あたらしい パソコンを かいましたよ。kyonen atarashii pasokon o kaimashita yo.Kim: I bought a new computer last year.
どこで かいましたか。doko de kaimashita ka.Ben: Where did you buy it?
がっこうの ちかくの みせです。gakkou no chikaku no mise desu.Kim: It is a shop near the school.
ABCショップですか。ABC shoppu desu ka.Ben: Is it ABC Shop?
はい、そうです。hai, sou desu.Kim: Yes, that is right.
いくらぐらいですか。ikura gurai desu ka.Ben: About how much was it?
じゅうまんえんぐらいです。juuman en gurai desu.Kim: About 100,000 yen.
まいにち あさごはんを たべますか。mainichi asagohan o tabemasu ka.Ana: Do you eat breakfast every day?
はい、まいにち たべますよ。hai, mainichi tabemasu yo.Mari: Yes, I eat it every day.
なにを たべますか。nani o tabemasu ka.Ana: What do you eat?
パンと くだものです。pan to kudamono desu.Mari: Bread and fruit.
ぎゅうにゅうを のみますか。gyuunyuu o nomimasu ka.Ana: Do you drink milk?
いいえ、ぎゅうにゅうは のみません。iie, gyuunyuu wa nomimasen.Mari: No, I do not drink milk.
なにを のみますか。nani o nomimasu ka.Ana: What do you drink?
コーヒーです。ko-hi- desu.Mari: Coffee.

8.12 Which verb goes with which noun (extra lesson)

Most nouns in this chapter only fit one or two verbs, so learning them in pairs saves a lot of effort. Tabemasu goes with food: asagohan, hirugohan, bangohan, gohan, ra-men and pan. Nomimasu goes with drinks, including mizu, ocha, koucha, gyuunyuu, ko-hi-, ko-ra, ju-su, osake, bi-ru, wain, su-pu and kusuri (medicine).

Yomimasu goes with reading materials: shousetsu, zasshi, shinbun and hon. Kikimasu goes with ongaku and uta, and mimasu goes with nyu-su, eiga and terebi. Kakimasu goes with repo-to, me-ru and tegami. Utaimasu goes with uta, suimasu with tabako and kakemasu with denwa. Kaimasu and urimasu are opposites and can take almost any thing.

Hanashimasu and oshiemasu work differently. Hanashimasu usually takes a person with to or ni, or a language with de. Oshiemasu takes a person with ni and a subject with o. When you are not sure which verb a noun needs, think about what you do with it: you eat food, drink a drink and read a text.

ラーメンを たべます。ra-men o tabemasu.I eat ramen.
みずを のみます。mizu o nomimasu.I drink water.
おちゃを のみます。ocha o nomimasu.I drink tea.
ビールを のみます。bi-ru o nomimasu.I drink beer.
くすりを のみます。kusuri o nomimasu.I take medicine.
ざっしを よみます。zasshi o yomimasu.I read a magazine.
しんぶんを よみます。shinbun o yomimasu.I read a newspaper.
おんがくを ききます。ongaku o kikimasu.I listen to music.
ニュースを みます。nyu-su o mimasu.I watch the news.
えいがを みます。eiga o mimasu.I watch a movie.
てがみを かきます。tegami o kakimasu.I write a letter.
うたを うたいます。uta o utaimasu.I sing a song.
タバコを すいます。tabako o suimasu.I smoke cigarettes.
くつを かいます。kutsu o kaimasu.I buy shoes.
くつを うります。kutsu o urimasu.I sell shoes.
がくせいに えいごを おしえます。gakusei ni eigo o oshiemasu.I teach English to the students.
えいごで はなします。eigo de hanashimasu.I speak in English.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
De: place, method or tool

  • de has three jobs in this chapter. Place: kissaten de (at the coffee shop). Method: eigo de (in English). Tool: hashi de (with chopsticks).
  • Ask the question to sort them out. doko de is place, douyatte is method and nani de is tool.
  • Language words, phone and TV are methods. Things you hold in your hand are tools.
  • Do not put no before de: say eigo de, never eigo no de.

De or ni with a place

  • de goes with an action verb: kaisha de hatarakimasu (work at the company).
  • ni goes with imasu and arimasu: kaisha ni imasu (be at the company).
  • Ask yourself whether something happens there (de) or someone is there (ni).

Ni or to

  • ni is for the person who receives the action: tomodachi ni denwa o kakemasu (call a friend).
  • to is for the person who does it with you: tomodachi to eiga o mimasu (watch a movie with a friend).
  • hanashimasu can take both: shachou to hanashimashita (spoke with) and okaasan ni hanashimashita (spoke to).
  • issho ni goes with to, as in ane to issho ni.

To for with, and to for and

  • After a person and right before the verb, to means with: kazoku to tabemashita.
  • Between two nouns, to means and: pan to kudamono (bread and fruit).

O or wa in a negative sentence

  • o is neutral: shousetsu o yomimasen.
  • wa puts the spotlight on the thing you do not do: wain wa nomimasen (wine is the thing I skip).
  • Both are correct. wa is common when you compare two things.
  • The object marker is written を but sounds like o. The topic marker is written は but sounds like wa.

Ni with time words

  • A specific time takes ni: nichiyoubi ni, kuji ni.
  • Non-specific words take no ni: maiasa, maiban, mainichi, maishuu, kesa and kinou.
  • kara, made and goro never take ni.
  • A length of time takes no marker at all: ichinenkan benkyoushimashita.
  • isshuukan ni ikkai is different, because ni means per there.

Goro or gurai

  • goro is around a point in time: kuji goro (around 9 o'clock).
  • gurai is about an amount: nijikan gurai (about 2 hours), juuman en gurai (about 100,000 yen).
  • donogurai and ikura gurai ask about an amount, so they use gurai.

Kikimasu: listen or ask

  • A thing with o means listen: ongaku o kikimasu.
  • A person with ni means ask: sensei ni kikimasu.

Hanashimasu with three markers

  • A person with to means talk with: shachou to hanashimasu.
  • A person with ni means talk to: okaasan ni hanashimasu.
  • A language with de means speak in it: eigo de hanashimasu.

Mimasu covers three meanings

  • mimasu means watch, look or see: eiga o mimasu, nyu-su o mimasu.
  • English uses three verbs where Japanese uses one, so look at the object to pick the English word.

Kakimasu, kaimasu and kakemasu

  • kakimasu is write: me-ru o kakimasu.
  • kaimasu is buy: kutsu o kaimasu.
  • kakemasu is call: denwa o kakemasu.
  • Only one sound changes, so say the noun first and the verb will follow.

Mimasu, nomimasu and yomimasu

  • All three end in mimasu.
  • mimasu is watch, nomimasu is drink and yomimasu is read.
  • Think of the object: eiga, mizu, shinbun.

Kikimasu and kakimasu

  • Only the first sound changes. Kiki is listen or ask, and kaki is write.

Kaimasu, urimasu and utaimasu

  • kaimasu is buy and urimasu is sell, so they are opposites.
  • urimasu (sell) and utaimasu (sing) both start with u.
  • uta is a song and utaimasu is to sing. You sing a song: uta o utaimasu.

Look-alike food and drink words

  • ocha is tea and koucha is black tea.
  • gohan is a meal or cooked rice. Add asa, hiru or ban to say which meal.
  • osake is alcohol in general. bi-ru and wain are two kinds of it.
  • tabemono, nomimono and yomimono all end in mono, which means thing. They are things to eat, to drink and to read.

Zenzen and the time words

  • zenzen always needs a negative ending: zenzen nomimasen.
  • itsumo, tokidoki and mainichi go with a positive verb: tokidoki nomimasu.
  • ototoi and yuube are in the past, so the verb ends in mashita or masen deshita.

Question words

  • nani o is what, doko de is where, dare ni is to whom, dare to is with whom, douyatte is how and nani de is with what tool.
  • donata is the polite form of dare.
  • The question word keeps the same marker its answer will take.

Eiga and eigakan

  • eiga is a movie and eigakan is a movie theater.
  • You watch a movie (eiga o mimasu) at the theater (eigakan de).

Words that start the same

  • hayai (early, fast), hatarakimasu (work), hajimarimasu (start), hanashimasu (speak), hashi (chopsticks), hanami (flower viewing) and hanabi (fireworks) all start with ha.
  • hanashimasu starts like hana (flower) but has nothing to do with it. Only hanami and hanabi are about flowers.
  • yasui (cheap), yasumimasu (rest), hiruyasumi (lunch break) and yasashii (kind, easy) share yasu. yasui is about price, yasumi is about resting and yasashii is about people and easy things.
  • Many words start with o. Sort them by type: okimasu, owarimasu and oshiemasu are verbs, osoi, omoi, omoshiroi, ookii and oishii are adjectives, and ocha and osake are drinks.

Where the katakana words come from

  • Katakana is for words borrowed from other languages, and most of the katakana words in Chapters 6 to 8 come from English: beddo, tesuto, me-ru, repo-to, ko-hi-, ju-su, bi-ru, wain, supu-n and nyu-su.
  • A few do not. ra-men comes from Chinese, pan (bread) and tabako (cigarette) come from Portuguese, and karaoke mixes Japanese and English.
  • biru (building) and bi-ru (beer) differ only in the long vowel, so watch the dash.

title: Going Places and the Dictionary Form
intro: Chapter 9 teaches you how to say where you go and where you come from. You learn the motion verbs ikimasu, kimasu, kaerimasu and modorimasu, and the markers that go with them: e or ni for the destination, de for the vehicle, to for the companion, de for the number of people, and ni, kara, made and goro for time. You also learn the ending words ne and yo, then meet the dictionary form, the casual twin of every masu verb, and the rules for changing from one form to the other.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
9.1 Destination e or ni, and origin kara kimashita (bunkei 9.1)

Chapter 9 is about moving from one place to another. The first pattern says where someone goes. It is A wa destination e or ni, followed by a motion verb. The four motion verbs are ikimasu (go), kimasu (come), kaerimasu (go home or return) and modorimasu (go back).

After the place you can use e or ni, and the book says the two are interchangeable. E stresses the direction, as in heading toward a place. Ni stresses the point where you arrive. The marker e is written へ in kana, but it is read e, not he. Do not mix it up with the ni that marks a time, as in kuji ni (at nine o'clock). After a place word, ni means to.

Kaerimasu and modorimasu both mean to return, but they are not the same. Kaerimasu is going home, to the place where you live or belong, such as your house or your home country. Modorimasu is going back to a place you were at before, such as a station or an office.

To say where someone comes from, use place + kara + kimashita. Furansu kara kimashita is I came from France. Kara kimashita is a set phrase, and it answers the question doko kara kimashita ka (where did you come from).

The last row uses to between two places, and there it means and. That is a different job from the to that means with, which comes in 9.4.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
わたしは にほんへ いきます。watashi wa nihon e ikimasu.I will go to Japan.
ともだちは いえに きました。tomodachi wa ie ni kimashita.My friend came to my house.
わたしは えいがかんへ いきます。watashi wa eigakan e ikimasu.I will go to the movie theater.
ぶちょうは にほんへ かえります。buchou wa nihon e kaerimasu.The department head will go home to Japan.

9.2 Mode of transportation de (bunkei 9.2)

Put de after a vehicle to say how you travel. Jitensha de is by bicycle, basu de is by bus and densha de is by train. The pattern is vehicle + de + motion verb. The one exception is aruite, which means on foot or by walking. It already carries the meaning of by, so it takes no de.

This de is not the place de from Chapter 8. In Chapter 8, de marked the place where an action happens, as in toshokan de benkyoushimashita (I studied at the library). Here de marks the vehicle you use to get somewhere. A quick check: if the word before de is a vehicle, de means by.

With a motion verb, the place you head to takes e or ni, never de. Compare the last two rows. Umi e ikimasu is I go to the sea, because ikimasu is a motion verb. Umi de oyogimasu is I swim in the sea, because oyogimasu is an activity at a place.

The question words for a vehicle are nani de and douyatte, and both mean how.

9.3 Time words ni, kara, made and goro (bunkei 9.3)

The time markers you met in Chapters 7 and 8 work the same way with motion verbs. Ni marks one exact time, such as a clock time, a day of the week or a date. Kara means from and made means until, so kuji kara goji made is from 9 until 5. Goro means around, and it goes straight after the time with no ni.

Words that are not an exact time take no ni. These include kinou, yuube, ototoi no yoru and maitoshi (every year). You say maitoshi firipin e ikimasu, never maitoshi ni.

The second row has ni (wa) after kusuriya. The wa in brackets is optional. It puts the spotlight on that one place, the same trick as o and wa in the negative sentences of Chapter 8. So kusuriya ni wa ikimasen deshita says I did not go to the drugstore, at least, and it hints that you went to other places.

Time words that point to the past, like kinou, yuube and ototoi, go with mashita or masen deshita. Watch the two jobs of kara. After a place, as in nihon kara, it means from a place. After a time, as in kuji kara, it means from a start time, and it goes with made.

9.4 Companion to or issho ni (bunkei 9.4)

The pattern is person + to (or to issho ni) + verb. It names the person who goes, comes or returns together with you. Issho ni only stresses the word together, so tomodachi to ikimasu and tomodachi to issho ni ikimasu mean the same thing.

This is the same to as in Chapter 8, where it also meant with. Remember that to has a second job: between two nouns or two places it means and. In su-pa- to ginkou e ikimashita, to means and. The way to tell them apart is the position. A to that comes right after a person and right before the verb means with.

For your own family, use the plain words such as haha and ane. For someone else's family, use the polite words such as okaasan and oneesan. The questions are dare to and the more polite donata to, both meaning with whom.

9.6 Question words for motion verbs

A question word takes the same marker its answer will take. Swap the question word for the real answer and the marker stays where it is. The book lists four question words for motion verbs. Two more question words are not on the book's list, but they are natural partners of the same markers. Doko kara asks where from, and nanji goro asks around what time. They are the first six rows. After them come the book's five question and answer pairs.

9.9 Masu form and dictionary form: two forms of every verb

Every verb has two forms. So far you have used the formal one, which ends in masu. The other is the dictionary form, the one you look up in a dictionary. It sounds casual, so the book also calls it the informal form. The meaning is the same, and only the politeness changes. Compare ongaku o kikimasu with ongaku o kiku.

If you cut masu off a formal verb, what is left is the stem. The book calls it the pre-masu form or the stem form. For nomimasu the stem is nomi. The stem is the middle step when you change from one form to the other.

The book sorts every verb into one of three types, and the names are the book's own. Irregular verbs have a stem that ends in an i sound, and the last sound shifts when the form changes, as in nomimasu and kakimasu. Regular verbs have a stem that ends in e, and you only add or drop ru, as in tabemasu. Special verbs have fixed forms that you simply memorize, and they are shimasu (do) and kimasu (come). Other books call the book's irregular verbs u-verbs and its regular verbs ru-verbs. The names differ, but the verbs are the same.

9.10 From masu form to dictionary form (page 137)

To go from the masu form to the dictionary form, you first remove masu to get the stem. What you do next depends on the type.

For Irregular verbs, change the last sound of the stem from the i row to the u row. Nomi becomes nomu, and kaki becomes kaku. The table below shows every shift: mi to mu, ki to ku, gi to gu, shi to su, chi to tsu, i to u, ni to nu, bi to bu and ri to ru. Notice that chi becomes tsu and not chu. For Regular verbs, add ru to the stem. Tabe becomes taberu, and mi becomes miru. Special verbs have no steps, so shimasu is always suru and kimasu is always kuru.

There is a catch when you go in this direction. A few Regular verbs also end in imasu, such as mimasu and okimasu. From the masu form alone you cannot always tell, so learn those as pairs. And kaerimasu looks like it could be Regular, but it is Irregular, so the dictionary form is kaeru.

9.11 From dictionary form to masu form (page 138)

Going the other way, from the dictionary form to the masu form, you look at the ending of the dictionary form first.

Irregular verbs end in bu, mu, nu, gu, su, ku, u, tsu, or ru after a, u or o. Change the last sound from the u row to the i row, and then add masu. Nomu becomes nomi, and then nomimasu. The book's step box leaves out u and tsu, but its table on the next page includes them, so kau becomes kaimasu and matsu becomes machimasu.

Regular verbs end in eru or iru. Remove ru and add masu. Taberu becomes tabe, and then tabemasu. Special verbs are fixed: suru is shimasu and kuru is kimasu.

9.13 The motion verbs and their four forms (extra lesson)

The four motion verbs follow the same four endings as every other masu verb: masu, masen, mashita and masen deshita. Ikimasu becomes ikimasen, ikimashita and ikimasen deshita. There is one split that matters a lot. Verbs of going use e or ni for the place you head to. 9.15 Phrases from the readings (extra lesson)

The review pages of this chapter have two readings: a summer trip to Singapore and Malaysia, and a letter from Jon to Ana. They are full of lines you can borrow when you write about your own trips. The rows below are lines from the two readings.

Watch the markers as you read. Ryokou o shimashita uses o with shimasu, so it means took a trip. Kakarimasu is a new verb that means takes, as in takes time, and it goes with a length of time that has no marker. Shuppatsu wa shigatsu tooka desu uses wa to make the departure the topic, and the date is simply the answer.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
E or ni after a place, ni after a time

  • After a place word, e and ni both mean to: umi e ikimasu or umi ni ikimasu (go to the sea).
  • After a time word, ni means at or on: kuji ni ikimasu (go at nine o'clock).
  • The two ni look the same but do different jobs. Ask yourself whether the word before it is a place or a time.
  • e stresses the direction. ni stresses the point where you arrive. In everyday speech they are interchangeable.

E or de with a place

  • Going to a place takes e or ni: umi e ikimasu (go to the sea).
  • Doing something at a place takes de: umi de oyogimasu (swim in the sea).
  • Ask whether the verb moves you to the place or whether the action happens there. Motion verbs take e. Activity verbs take de.
  • kaimonoshimasu, asobimasu, oyogimasu and benkyoushimasu are activity verbs, so they take de.

De for a vehicle, de for a number of people

  • Look at the word before de. A vehicle says how you travel: basu de (by bus).
  • A number of people says how many of you go: sannin de (three of us).
  • Both can be in one sentence: sannin de basu de ikimasu (the three of us go by bus).
  • aruite (on foot) already says how you travel, so it never takes de.

To for with, and to for and

  • to right before the verb means with: tomodachi to ikimasu (go with a friend).
  • to between two places or nouns means and: su-pa- to ginkou e ikimashita (went to the supermarket and the bank).
  • issho ni backs up the with meaning: tomodachi to issho ni ikimasu. issho ni alone never replaces to.

Kara for a place, kara for a time

  • A place plus kara plus kimashita means came from: furansu kara kimashita (came from France).
  • A time plus kara plus made means from and until: kuji kara goji made (from nine to five).
  • kara and made also work with places: shingapo-ru kara mare-shia made (from Singapore to Malaysia).

Ni with time words

  • An exact time or a day takes ni: kuji ni, getsuyoubi ni, juunigatsu nijuugonichi ni.
  • Habit and relative words take no ni: kinou, yuube, ototoi, maitoshi, kongetsu, sengetsu, raishuu, konban and kotoshi.
  • goro never takes ni: sanji goro kimashita (came around three).
  • A length of time takes no marker at all: basu de sanjikan kakarimasu (it takes three hours by bus).

The marker e is read e

  • The marker is written with the kana for he, but it is read e.
  • nihon e ikimasu is read nihon e ikimasu, never nihon he ikimasu.
  • The same thing happens with wa (written with the kana for ha) and o (written with the kana for wo).
  • Inside a word the kana still says he. henji (reply) and heya (room) start with he.

Ikimasu and kimasu

  • ikimasu is go and kimasu is come. They take the same markers.
  • Only the direction changes: watashi wa nihon e ikimasu (I go to Japan) and tomodachi wa ie e kimashita (my friend came to my house).
  • kara goes with kimashita when you say where you came from.

Ikimasu and imasu

  • The two sounds are one letter apart.
  • ikimasu is go. imasu is to be somewhere, used for people and animals.
  • imasu appears in the readings, as in shingapo-ru ni imasu (be in Singapore).

Kaerimasu or modorimasu

  • kaerimasu is go home, to where you live or belong: nihon e kaerimasu (go home to Japan).
  • modorimasu is go back to a place you were at before, such as a station or an office: eki ni modorimasu.
  • Both are fine for return. kaerimasu is the one you will use most.

Kaerimasu, kaimasu and kakemasu

  • The three are one sound apart.
  • kaerimasu is go home, kaimasu is buy and kakemasu is call (a phone).
  • Check the markers: a place with e goes with kaerimasu, a thing with o goes with kaimasu, and denwa o goes with kakemasu.

Kimasu, kikimasu and kirimasu

  • kimasu is come, kikimasu is listen or ask, and kirimasu is cut.
  • kimasu is a Special verb. kikimasu and kirimasu are Irregular verbs.
  • In the dictionary form they are kuru, kiku and kiru. Do not mix up kuru and kiru.

Asobimasu and oyogimasu

  • Both are activity verbs, so they take de for the place.
  • asobimasu is play or enjoy yourself, and oyogimasu is swim.
  • kouen de asobimasu (play in the park) and umi de oyogimasu (swim in the sea).

Counting people

  • hitori (1) and futari (2) are special words.
  • From three on it is the number plus nin: sannin, yonin, gonin, rokunin, hachinin, kyuunin, juunin.
  • Four is yonin, never shinin. Seven is shichinin or nananin.
  • The count includes you. futari de is two people in all, and hitori de is alone.
  • For how many people, say nannin de ikimashita ka.

Goro or gurai

  • goro is around a point in time: kuji goro (around nine o'clock).
  • gurai is about an amount of time: sanjikan gurai (about three hours).
  • goro goes with a clock time, and gurai goes with a length of time.
  • nanji goro asks around what time. nanjikan gurai asks about how long.

Nani de or douyatte

  • Both ask how you travel, and both are answered with a vehicle plus de.
  • nani de ikimasu ka and douyatte ikimasu ka get the same answer: basu de ikimasu.
  • dare to asks with whom, and nannin de asks how many people.
  • doko e asks where to. It has the same job as doko ni.

Ne or yo

  • ne asks the other person to agree: atsui desu ne (it is hot, isn't it?).
  • yo tells the other person something, or stresses it: indojin desu yo (I am Indian, you know).
  • The usual reply to ne is sou desu ne, which means yes, I agree.
  • yo can also correct someone: iie, asatte desu yo (no, it is the day after tomorrow!).

Masu form and dictionary form

  • The masu form is formal. The dictionary form is casual, and it is the form you look up in a dictionary.
  • The meaning is the same. Only the politeness changes.
  • The stem is what is left when you remove masu. nomimasu has the stem nomi.
  • The stem is the middle step when you change from one form to the other.

Which type is it?

  • Check the dictionary form first. A verb that ends in eru or iru is probably Regular.
  • Every other ending (bu, mu, nu, gu, su, ku, u, tsu, ru after a, u or o) is Irregular.
  • suru and kuru are Special, and so is a noun plus suru, such as benkyousuru.
  • Always check the traps in the next two topics.

Traps: eru or iru that is not Regular

  • kaeru ends in eru, but it is Irregular. It becomes kaerimasu, never kaemasu.
  • The book names hairu, hashiru, kiru and shiru as the same kind of trap.
  • Learn them as pairs: kaeru and kaerimasu, hairu and hairimasu.

Traps: ending in imasu but Regular

  • mimasu and okimasu end in imasu, but they are Regular verbs.
  • Just add ru: mimasu becomes miru, and okimasu becomes okiru.
  • From the masu form alone you cannot always tell, so learn those two as pairs.

Endings that change in surprising ways

  • A verb ending in u changes u to i before masu: suu becomes suimasu and kau becomes kaimasu.
  • A verb ending in tsu changes tsu to chi: matsu becomes machimasu.
  • A verb ending in nu changes nu to ni: shinu becomes shinimasu.
  • A verb ending in su changes su to shi: hanasu becomes hanashimasu.

Iku is starred in the book

  • The book puts a star on iku, in the same note as kaeru and shiru.
  • The rule still works for iku: ku changes to ki, so you get ikimasu.
  • kaeru is the real trap. iku does not catch you out.

One word, more than one meaning

  • kaerimasu means go home or return: nihon e kaerimasu.
  • hayai means fast or early: takushi- wa hayai desu yo (the taxi is fast).
  • kakarimasu means takes (time): gojikan kakarimasu (it takes five hours).

Past time words

  • kinou, yuube, ototoi, sengetsu and kyonen point to the past.
  • The verb then ends in mashita or masen deshita.
  • ashita, raishuu, raigetsu and konban point to the present or future, so the verb ends in masu or masen.

Places that look alike

  • bijutsukan, eigakan and toshokan all end in kan, a building: museum, movie theater and library.
  • ryokan is a Japanese style inn. ryokou is a trip.
  • inaka, machi and mura are the countryside, a town and a village.
  • kawa, ike and umi are a river, a pond and the sea.
  • gaikoku is a foreign country. kaigai is overseas.
  • otera and onsen are a temple and a hot spring.

9hai, tokidoki ikimasu. tomodachi to ikimasu. (はい、ときどき いきます。ともだちと いきます。)dare to asks with whom. Sample meaning: Yes, sometimes. I go with friends.
10hai, ikimashita. shingapo-ru e ikimashita. (はい、いきました。シンガポールへ いきました。)doko e asks where to. Sample meaning: Yes, I went. I went to Singapore.

Translate into Japanese (page 145)

Word order can shift a little in all of these, as long as the verb stays last.

#AnswerWhy

title: Casual Speech and Informal Verbs
intro: Chapter 10 teaches you how to speak casually, the way you talk with family and close friends. You learn to build noun + suru verbs, and the four informal verb forms: the dictionary form (present positive), the nai form (present negative), the ta form (past positive) and the nakatta form (past negative). You sort verbs into Groups 1 to 5, Regular verbs and Special verbs, learn how to change between the formal and casual styles, and meet the casual question ending no and the soft ending wa that women often use.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
10.1 Noun + suru (bunkei 10.1, page 148)

Many actions in Japanese are said with a noun plus suru. The noun names the action, and suru does the job of the verb, much like the English word do. The noun benkyou means study, and benkyoushimasu is the verb to study. The formal form is shimasu, and the casual form, which you meet later in this chapter, is suru.

The book writes the noun and shimasu together as one word, as in untenshimasu (drive) and soujishimasu (clean). The ending behaves just like shimasu, so you get shimasen, shimashita and shimasen deshita. Other markers work as usual. The person you do something to takes ni, as in kachou ni setsumeishimashita. The thing you do something to takes o, as in heya o soujishimasu.

Sports and games also take suru. For example, tenisushimashita means played tennis, and gorufushimasu means play golf. Do not use asobimasu for a sport. The list below shows every noun + suru verb in the book, and then the book's example sentences.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
よやくします、よやくするyoyakushimasu, yoyakusurureserve
しょうかいします、しょうかいするshoukaishimasu, shoukaisuruintroduce

へんじします、へんじするhenjishimasu, henjisurureply
そうじします、そうじするsoujishimasu, soujisuruclean

せんたくします、せんたくするsentakushimasu, sentakusurudo laundry

かいものします、かいものするkaimonoshimasu, kaimonosurushop
せつめいします、せつめいするsetsumeishimasu, setsumeisuruexplain
でんわします、でんわするdenwashimasu, denwasurucall
うんてんします、うんてんするuntenshimasu, untensurudrive
