にほんで にほんごを べんきょうしました。nihon de nihongo o benkyoushimashita.I studied Japanese in Japan.
かちょうに せつめいしました。kachou ni setsumeishimashita.I explained it to the section head.
にちようびに へやを そうじします。nichiyoubi ni heya o soujishimasu.I clean my room on Sunday.
ゆうべ じゅうじまで ざんぎょうしました。yuube juuji made zangyoushimashita.Last night I worked overtime until ten.
がくせいに あたらしい せんせいを しょうかいします。gakusei ni atarashii sensei o shoukaishimasu.I will introduce the new teacher to the students.
きょねん かぞくと りょこうしましたか。kyonen kazoku to ryokoushimashita ka.Did you travel with your family last year?
ちかくの デパートで かいものしました。chikaku no depa-to de kaimonoshimashita.I shopped at a department store nearby.
あさって アナさんに でんわします。asatte ana san ni denwashimasu.I will call Ana the day after tomorrow.
まいあさ れんしゅうします。maiasa renshuushimasu.I practice every morning.
たなかさんに へんじしませんでした。tanaka san ni henjishimasen deshita.I did not reply to Mr. Tanaka.
なんじから しごとしますか。nanji kara shigotoshimasu ka.What time do you start work?
おととい ともだちと テニスしました。ototoi tomodachi to tenisushimashita.I played tennis with a friend the day before yesterday.
やまださんは まいつき ゴルフします。yamada san wa maitsuki gorufushimasu.Mr. Yamada plays golf every month.

10.2 Informal verbs: the four forms (page 149)

In Chapter 7 you learned four formal verb endings: masu, masen, mashita and masen deshita. Every verb also has four informal forms. They mean the same thing, but they sound more casual, and you use them with family, close friends and people your own age or younger. With a teacher, a boss or someone you have just met, keep using the formal forms.

The four informal forms have names in the book. The present positive is the dictionary form, which you learned in Chapter 9. The present negative is the nai form. The past positive is the ta form. The past negative is the nakatta form. For owaru (finish) they are owaru, owaranai, owatta and owaranakatta.

The way each form is made depends on the type of verb. The book has three types: Irregular verbs (the book's name for the verbs that end in u in the dictionary form, such as nomu), Regular verbs (the ones that end in eru or iru, such as taberu) and Special verbs (suru and kuru). The Irregular verbs are split into five groups, and the next lessons go through them one by one. In every group the present negative ends in nai, the past positive ends in ta or da, and the past negative is the nai form with the last i changed to katta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
おわりますowarimasufinish (formal, present positive)
おわるowarufinish (informal, dictionary form)
おわりませんowarimasenwill not finish (formal, present negative)
おわらないowaranaiwill not finish (informal, nai form)
おわりましたowarimashitafinished (formal, past positive)
おわったowattafinished (informal, ta form)
おわりませんでしたowarimasen deshitadid not finish (formal, past negative)
おわらなかったowaranakattadid not finish (informal, nakatta form)
かいぎは さんじに おわります。kaigi wa sanji ni owarimasu.The meeting ends at three. (formal)
かいぎは さんじに おわる。kaigi wa sanji ni owaru.The meeting ends at three. (informal)

10.3 Group 1: verbs that end in bu, mu or nu (page 149)

Group 1 has the verbs whose dictionary form ends in bu, mu or nu. To make the nai form, change the last u sound to the a sound and add nai: bu becomes ba, mu becomes ma, and nu becomes na. So asobu becomes asobanai, nomu becomes nomanai, and shinu becomes shinanai.

For the ta form, bu, mu and nu all change to the same ending, nda. So asobu becomes asonda, nomu becomes nonda, and shinu becomes shinda. The past negative takes the nai form and changes nai to nakatta, so you get asobanakatta, nomanakatta and shinanakatta.

Because so many verbs end in nda, the ta form alone does not tell you the dictionary form. A form such as yonda could come from yomu (read) or from yobu (call), so context decides.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
あそぶ、あそばない、あそんだ、あそばなかったasobu, asobanai, asonda, asobanakattaplay
のむ、のまない、のんだ、のまなかったnomu, nomanai, nonda, nomanakattadrink
よむ、よまない、よんだ、よまなかったyomu, yomanai, yonda, yomanakattaread
やすむ、やすまない、やすんだ、やすまなかったyasumu, yasumanai, yasunda, yasumanakattatake a holiday, rest
しぬ、しなない、しんだ、しななかったshinu, shinanai, shinda, shinanakattadie
ともだちと あそぶ。tomodachi to asobu.I play with a friend.
コーヒーを のんだ。ko-hi- o nonda.I drank coffee.
しんぶんを よまない。shinbun o yomanai.I do not read the newspaper.
みっかから むいかまで やすんだ。mikka kara muika made yasunda.I took a holiday from the 3rd to the 6th.
ともだちと あそばなかった。tomodachi to asobanakatta.I did not play with a friend.

10.4 Group 2: verbs that end in gu (page 149)

Group 2 has the verbs that end in gu. The verb oyogu (swim) is the only one of this group in your vocabulary. For the nai form, gu becomes ga plus nai, so oyogu becomes oyoganai.

The ta form is different from Group 1. The ending gu changes to ida, so oyogu becomes oyoida. Do not say oyoinda or oyonda. The past negative is oyoganakatta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
およぐ、およがない、およいだ、およがなかったoyogu, oyoganai, oyoida, oyoganakattaswim
あいみさんは およがない。aimi san wa oyoganai.Aimi does not swim.
きのう うみで およいだ。kinou umi de oyoida.I swam in the sea yesterday.
かわで およがなかった。kawa de oyoganakatta.I did not swim in the river.
まいあさ かわで およぐ。maiasa kawa de oyogu.I swim in the river every morning.

10.5 Group 3: verbs that end in su (page 149)

Group 3 has the verbs that end in su, such as hanasu (speak) and dasu (submit). For the nai form, su becomes sa plus nai, as in hanasanai and dasanai.

The ta form changes su to shita. So hanasu becomes hanashita, and dasu becomes dashita. Notice that hanashita looks like the ta form of suru (shita, did), but the verb here is hanasu and the sound hana comes first. The past negative is hanasanakatta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
はなす、はなさない、はなした、はなさなかったhanasu, hanasanai, hanashita, hanasanakattaspeak, talk
だす、ださない、だした、ださなかったdasu, dasanai, dashita, dasanakattasubmit, send, take out
たなかさんと はなす。tanaka san to hanasu.I talk with Mr. Tanaka.
たなかさんと はなした。tanaka san to hanashita.I talked with Mr. Tanaka.
きのう レポートを ださなかった。kinou repo-to o dasanakatta.I did not submit the report yesterday.
まいにち レポートを だす。mainichi repo-to o dasu.I submit a report every day.

10.6 Group 4: verbs that end in ku (page 149)

Group 4 has the verbs that end in ku, such as kaku (write), kiku (listen or ask), hataraku (work) and aruku (walk). For the nai form, ku becomes ka plus nai, as in kakanai and kikanai.

The ta form changes ku to ita. So kaku becomes kaita, kiku becomes kiita, and hataraku becomes hataraita. The past negative is kakanakatta.

There is one important exception. The verb iku (go) ends in ku, but the book does not put it in this group. It is starred and listed in Group 5, because its ta form is itta, not iita. Its nai form is ordinary, ikanai, and its past negative is ikanakatta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
かく、かかない、かいた、かかなかったkaku, kakanai, kaita, kakanakattawrite
きく、きかない、きいた、きかなかったkiku, kikanai, kiita, kikanakattalisten, ask
はたらく、はたらかない、はたらいた、はたらかなかったhataraku, hatarakanai, hataraita, hatarakanakattawork
あるく、あるかない、あるいた、あるかなかったaruku, arukanai, aruita, arukanakattawalk
いく、いかない、いった、いかなかったiku, ikanai, itta, ikanakattago (starred: it sits in Group 5)
メールを かいた。me-ru o kaita.I wrote an email.
やまだせんせいに きいた。yamada sensei ni kiita.I asked Teacher Yamada.
にほんで はたらいた。nihon de hataraita.I worked in Japan.
きょねん にほんに いった。kyonen nihon ni itta.I went to Japan last year.
ともだちの たんじょうびパーティー(へ) いかなかった。tomodachi no tanjoubi pa-ti- (e) ikanakatta.I did not go to my friend's birthday party.

10.7 Group 5: verbs that end in u, tsu or ru (page 149)

Group 5 is the biggest group. It has the verbs that end in u (kau, utau, suu), in tsu (matsu, motsu) and in ru (wakaru, uru, tsukuru, hajimaru, owaru, hairu). Three different endings, but one shared result: the ta form of all of them ends in tta.

For the ta form, u, tsu and ru all become tta. So kau becomes katta, matsu becomes matta, and wakaru becomes wakatta. For the nai form, the last sound changes to the a row, but there are two things to watch. A verb that ends in u takes wa, not a, so kau becomes kawanai and suu becomes suwanai. A verb that ends in tsu takes ta, so matsu becomes matanai. A verb that ends in ru takes ra, so wakaru becomes wakaranai.

Two verbs in this group are starred in the book because they look like something else. The verb iku (go) is listed here because its ta form is itta, like the others. The verb kaeru (go home) ends in eru, which makes it look Regular, but it follows the Group 5 rules, so it is kaeranai and kaetta. The book's footnote adds shiru (know), hairu (enter), hashiru (run) and kiru (cut) to the same list. These verbs all end in eru or iru but belong to Group 5, so they are shiranai, hairanai, hashiranai and kiranai, and shitta, haitta, hashitta and kitta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
かう、かわない、かった、かわなかったkau, kawanai, katta, kawanakattabuy
うたう、うたわない、うたった、うたわなかったutau, utawanai, utatta, utawanakattasing
すう、すわない、すった、すわなかったsuu, suwanai, sutta, suwanakattasmoke
まつ、またない、まった、またなかったmatsu, matanai, matta, matanakattawait
もつ、もたない、もった、もたなかったmotsu, motanai, motta, motanakattahold, carry
わかる、わからない、わかった、わからなかったwakaru, wakaranai, wakatta, wakaranakattaunderstand
うる、うらない、うった、うらなかったuru, uranai, utta, uranakattasell
つくる、つくらない、つくった、つくらなかったtsukuru, tsukuranai, tsukutta, tsukuranakattamake, cook
かえる、かえらない、かえった、かえらなかったkaeru, kaeranai, kaetta, kaeranakattago home (the exception)
しる、しらない、しった、しらなかったshiru, shiranai, shitta, shiranakattaknow (the exception)
あたらしいパソコンを かった。atarashii pasokon o katta.I bought a new computer.
くつを かわない。kutsu o kawanai.I do not buy shoes.
タバコを すわない。tabako o suwanai.I do not smoke.
かいぎは さんじに はじまる。kaigi wa sanji ni hajimaru.The meeting starts at three.
けいたいを うった。keitai o utta.I sold my cell phone.
らいねん にほんへ かえる。rainen nihon e kaeru.I will go home to Japan next year.
きのう にほんへ かえった。kinou nihon e kaetta.I went home to Japan yesterday.

10.8 Regular verbs: eru and iru (page 149)

Regular verbs end in eru or iru in the dictionary form, and they are the easiest to change. To make the nai form, drop ru and add nai. To make the ta form, drop ru and add ta. For the past negative, drop ru and add nakatta. For example, taberu becomes tabenai, tabeta and tabenakatta, and miru becomes minai, mita and minakatta.

There is no change in the last sound, so you never have to think about nda, tta or ita. The only trouble is knowing which verbs are Regular. The rule is that a verb that ends in eru or iru is Regular, with the exceptions in Group 5: kaeru, shiru, hairu, hashiru and kiru. The verb okiru (wake up) ends in iru and is Regular, so it is okinai and okita.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
たべる、たべない、たべた、たべなかったtaberu, tabenai, tabeta, tabenakattaeat
みる、みない、みた、みなかったmiru, minai, mita, minakattawatch, look
ねる、ねない、ねた、ねなかったneru, nenai, neta, nenakattasleep
おきる、おきない、おきた、おきなかったokiru, okinai, okita, okinakattawake up
おしえる、おしえない、おしえた、おしえなかったoshieru, oshienai, oshieta, oshienakattateach, tell
かける、かけない、かけた、かけなかったkakeru, kakenai, kaketa, kakenakattamake (a phone call)
おぼえる、おぼえない、おぼえた、おぼえなかったoboeru, oboenai, oboeta, oboenakattaremember, memorize
あさごはんを たべない。asagohan o tabenai.I do not eat breakfast.
ともだちと えいがを みた。tomodachi to eiga o mita.I watched a movie with a friend.
けさ おそく おきた。kesa osoku okita.I got up late this morning.
アナさんに でんわを かけなかった。ana san ni denwa o kakenakatta.I did not call Ana.
だいがくで えいごを おしえる。daigaku de eigo o oshieru.I teach English at the university.

10.9 Special verbs: suru and kuru (page 149)

The two Special verbs are suru (do) and kuru (come), and their forms are fixed, so you simply memorize them. The forms of suru are suru, shinai, shita and shinakatta. The forms of kuru are kuru, konai, kita and konakatta.

Every noun + suru verb follows suru. So benkyousuru becomes benkyoushinai, benkyoushita and benkyoushinakatta. In the same way, tenisusuru becomes tenisushita.

Watch the first sound of kuru. In the dictionary form and the ta form it is ku and ki, but in the nai form and the nakatta form it is ko, as in konai and konakatta.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
する、しない、した、しなかったsuru, shinai, shita, shinakattado
くる、こない、きた、こなかったkuru, konai, kita, konakattacome
べんきょうする、べんきょうしない、べんきょうした、べんきょうしなかったbenkyousuru, benkyoushinai, benkyoushita, benkyoushinakattastudy
かいものする、かいものしない、かいものした、かいものしなかったkaimonosuru, kaimonoshinai, kaimonoshita, kaimonoshinakattashop
きのう べんきょうしなかった。kinou benkyoushinakatta.I did not study yesterday.
らいしゅう かいものしない。raishuu kaimonoshinai.I will not go shopping next week.
おととい ともだちと きた。ototoi tomodachi to kita.I came with a friend the day before yesterday.
おととい こなかった。ototoi konakatta.I did not come the day before yesterday.

10.10 Masu form to the dictionary form: present positive (page 151)

The first conversion is from masu to the dictionary form, the informal present positive. You already know how to do this from Chapter 9. Remove masu to get the stem, and then follow the rules for the verb type. For example, kaimonoshimasu becomes kaimonosuru, tabemasu becomes taberu, yomimasu becomes yomu, and yasumimasu becomes yasumu.

The dictionary form is also the casual way to talk about the future. The sentence ashita kaimonosuru means I will go shopping tomorrow. The same form covers habits, as in maiasa yomu (I read every morning).

In the book's examples some markers are put in brackets, such as (ni) and (o). That means they are often dropped in casual talk. Lesson 10.16 explains this.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
あした おかあさんと かいものします。ashita okaasan to kaimonoshimasu.I will go shopping with my mother tomorrow. (formal)
あした おかあさんと かいものする。ashita okaasan to kaimonosuru.I will go shopping with my mother tomorrow. (informal)
らいしゅうの げつようびに かちょうに そうだんします。raishuu no getsuyoubi ni kachou ni soudanshimasu.I will consult the section head on Monday next week. (formal)
らいしゅうの げつようび(に) かちょうに そうだんする。raishuu no getsuyoubi (ni) kachou ni soudansuru.I will consult the section head on Monday next week. (informal)
にほんの りょうりを たべます。nihon no ryouri o tabemasu.I eat Japanese food. (formal)
にほんの りょうり(を) たべる。nihon no ryouri (o) taberu.I eat Japanese food. (informal)
まいあさ にほんごの しんぶんを よみます。maiasa nihongo no shinbun o yomimasu.I read the Japanese newspaper every morning. (formal)
まいあさ にほんごの しんぶん(を) よむ。maiasa nihongo no shinbun (o) yomu.I read the Japanese newspaper every morning. (informal)
みっかから むいかまで やすみます。mikka kara muika made yasumimasu.I take a holiday from the 3rd to the 6th. (formal)
みっかから むいかまで やすむ。mikka kara muika made yasumu.I take a holiday from the 3rd to the 6th. (informal)

10.11 Masen to the nai form: present negative (page 151)

To make the informal present negative, change the verb to its nai form. The rule depends on the group. For Group 1 to Group 5, the final u sound changes to the a sound and nai is added (nomu becomes nomanai, kau becomes kawanai). For Regular verbs, drop ru and add nai (taberu becomes tabenai). For Special verbs, suru becomes shinai and kuru becomes konai.

The book gives two notes about markers in negative sentences. The first is that o sometimes changes into wa when the sentence turns negative, as in ko-hi- wa nomanai. The second is that wa can be added after ni and e in a negative sentence for more emphasis, as in goji niwa owaranai (it does not end at five, though).

Remember that the nai form is the casual twin of masen. It does not mean past tense.

10.12 Mashita to the ta form: past positive (page 152)

The ta form is the informal past positive. For Regular verbs, drop ru and add ta (okiru becomes okita). For Special verbs, suru becomes shita and kuru becomes kita. For the five Irregular groups, the ending depends on the last sound of the dictionary form:

  • bu, mu and nu become nda (yasumu becomes yasunda).
  • gu becomes ida (oyogu becomes oyoida).
  • su becomes shita (hanasu becomes hanashita).
  • ku becomes ita (kaku becomes kaita), except iku, which becomes itta.
  • u, tsu and ru become tta (kau becomes katta, matsu becomes matta, kaeru becomes kaetta).

10.13 Masen deshita to the nakatta form: past negative (page 152)

The nakatta form is the informal past negative. To make it, take the nai form and replace the final i with katta. So yomanai becomes yomanakatta, tabenai becomes tabenakatta, and konai becomes konakatta.

This works exactly like the past tense of an i-adjective, because nai itself behaves like an i-adjective. The word nai ends in i, and the past of nai is nakatta, in the same way that takai (expensive) becomes takakatta (was expensive).

Do not mix up the nai form and the nakatta form. The form tabenai means I do not eat, and tabenakatta means I did not eat.

10.16 Leaving out markers in casual speech (page 151)

In casual speech and writing, the markers o, ga, ni and e are sometimes left out. Say ko-hi- nomu instead of ko-hi- o nomu, and nihon iku instead of nihon e iku. The meaning does not change, because the listener can work out the job of the word from the situation.

The other markers are not dropped. The markers de (by, at), to (with), kara (from) and made (until) all carry meaning that the listener cannot guess, so they stay.

In negative sentences you may see two small changes. The marker o can turn into wa, and wa can be added after e and ni for extra emphasis. These changes are optional, and they are never required.

10.18 Casual questions with no (bunkei 10.2, page 155)

In casual speech, the question marker ka is replaced by no. The question ikimasu ka becomes iku no, and owarimashita ka becomes owatta no. The verb is in the informal form, and your voice goes up at the end of the sentence. In writing, a question mark shows that it is a question.

When a question word is used, no goes at the end in the same way. Questions such as doko e iku no (where are you going) and nani o tabeta no (what did you eat) are everyday casual questions. A question with only a question word, such as itsu (when), can stand alone.

Some of the book's casual questions, such as kaigi owatta no, end in a full stop, but they are still questions. The no marker is also used by both men and women. The soft wa in the next lesson is the one that is used mostly by women.

10.19 Ending marker wa for women (bunkei 10.3, page 155)

The ending wa is a soft ending that women often use to give an opinion, to make something clearer or to show a feeling. It goes at the end of a casual sentence. The book calls it an ending marker for a female speaker.

After a verb or an i-adjective, you add wa directly: iku wa, oishikatta wa. After a noun or a na-adjective, you add da first, so kirei desu becomes kirei da wa and igirisujin desu becomes igirisujin da wa. Remember that desu and masu are dropped, because the sentence is casual.

Be careful with the spelling. This ending is written わ in hiragana, and it is not the topic marker wa, which is written は. They sound the same, but they have different jobs. In the same sentence, you can see both, as in fujisan wa kirei da wa (Mount Fuji is beautiful).

10.23 Phrases from the readings (extra lesson)

The reading exercises at the end of the chapter include a trip to Sapporo and a letter from Ana to John. Many of their sentences are useful on their own. This table lists the key sentences so that you can read the passages with confidence and reuse the phrases. All the sentences in these passages are formal. Try changing each one to the informal form as extra practice.

Notice that the letter uses ordinary formal verbs in the past (mimashita, kaerimashita) and the present (zangyoushimasu), which is the normal style for a letter to a friend you do not speak to every day.

10.24 Which verb goes with which noun (extra lesson)

The new verbs in this chapter each have a few nouns they like to go with, and learning them in pairs makes the sentences come quicker. Most take their noun with o. Two are different: wakaru takes what you understand with ga, as in nihongo ga wakaru, and shiru is mostly used in the negative, as in ana san o shiranai (I don't know Ana).

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Noun or noun + suru

  • benkyou is the noun study. benkyoushimasu (formal) and benkyousuru (casual) are the verb to study.
  • The same goes for soudan, setsumei, unten, souji, sentaku and the rest. Add shimasu or suru to turn the noun into a verb.
  • The book writes the noun and shimasu together. The thing you do it to still takes o, as in heya o soujishimasu.

Sports take suru, not asobu

  • Say tenisushimasu or gorufushimasu to play a sport.
  • asobimasu means to play or to have fun, as in tomodachi to asobimasu. It is not used for a sport.

The five ta form endings

  • bu, mu and nu become nda: asobu, asonda. nomu, nonda. shinu, shinda.
  • gu becomes ida: oyogu, oyoida.
  • su becomes shita: hanasu, hanashita.
  • ku becomes ita: kaku, kaita. The one exception is iku, which becomes itta.
  • u, tsu and ru become tta: kau, katta. matsu, matta. wakaru, wakatta.
  • Regular verbs just drop ru and add ta: taberu, tabeta.

Iku ends in ku but sits in Group 5

  • every other verb that ends in ku becomes ita. kaku is kaita, and kiku is kiita.
  • iku becomes itta, not iita. The book marks it with a star and lists it in Group 5.
  • The nai form of iku is normal: ikanai. Only the ta form is special.

Kau and suu: the nai form uses wa

  • kau becomes kawanai, not kaanai.
  • suu becomes suwanai, not suanai.
  • utau becomes utawanai.
  • The verb ends in u, so the u changes to wa and then nai is added.
  • The ta form is normal: katta, sutta, utatta.

Kaeru, shiru, hairu, hashiru and kiru

  • all of them end in eru or iru, so they look Regular. They are really Group 5.
  • kaeru is kaeranai and kaetta. It is not kaenai and kaeta.
  • shiru is shiranai and shitta.
  • hairu is hairanai and haitta, hashiru is hashiranai and hashitta, and kiru is kiranai and kitta.
  • Regular look-alikes such as miru, okiru and taberu really are Regular.

Kiita, kita and kitta

  • kiita comes from kiku and means listened or asked.
  • kita comes from kuru and means came.
  • kitta comes from kiru and means cut.
  • The sounds are close, so listen for the small tsu and for the long ii.

Itta, hanashita and shita

  • itta is the ta form of iku, went.
  • hanashita is the ta form of hanasu, spoke. It ends in shita, but the verb is not suru.
  • shita on its own is the ta form of suru, did.

Nai or nakatta

  • nai is the present negative. tabenai means I do not eat.
  • nakatta is the past negative. tabenakatta means I did not eat.
  • To go from nai to nakatta, change the last i to katta.
  • Do not use nai for something that already happened.

One ta form, several verbs

  • yonda can be yomu (read) or yobu (call). nonda is nomu. asonda is asobu. yasunda is yasumu. shinda is shinu.
  • All of them end in nda. The sentence tells you which verb is meant.
  • katta is kau (buy). Do not mix it up with the ta form of an i-adjective, such as takakatta (was expensive).

Present and future use the same form

  • iku can mean I go or I will go. The time word tells you which one. ashita iku is I will go tomorrow.
  • A past time word needs the ta form: kinou itta.

Two ways to ask a casual question

  • With ka the verb must be in the masu form: ikimasu ka.
  • With no the verb is in the informal form: iku no.
  • You can also just raise your voice. iku? is enough between friends.
  • Keep the pairs together: ikimasu ka and iku no.

No as a question and no as of

  • ana san no tanjoubi is Ana's birthday. This no joins two nouns.
  • iku no is are you going. This no comes at the end of the sentence and asks a casual question.
  • The one at the end is always after an informal verb, an i-adjective, or nano after a noun or na-adjective.

Nano, no and dawa

  • After a verb or an i-adjective, use no or wa directly: iku no, takai wa.
  • After a noun or a na-adjective, use nano or dawa: igirisujin nano, kirei dawa.
  • A noun or na-adjective never takes da in front of the question no. Say kirei nano, not kirei da no.

Ending wa and topic wa

  • The ending wa for women is written わ. The topic marker is written は.
  • Both sound the same. fujisan wa kirei da wa has the topic wa first and the ending wa last.
  • The ending goes at the very end of the sentence. The topic marker goes after the topic.

Dropping markers

  • o, ga, ni and e are often dropped in casual talk. ko-hi- nomu is the same as ko-hi- o nomu.
  • de, to, kara and made are not dropped, because they carry meaning that cannot be guessed.
  • In negative sentences o can change to wa, and wa can be added after ni and e. These are optional.

Who to use informal forms with

  • Use the informal forms with family and close friends.
  • Use the formal forms with teachers, bosses and people you have just met.
  • Mixing the two in one conversation is a common mistake. Pick one style for each person.

Desu, da and janai

  • desu becomes da in casual speech: nihonjin da.
  • ja arimasen becomes janai, deshita becomes datta, and ja arimasen deshita becomes janakatta.
  • An i-adjective just loses its desu: takai desu becomes takai.
  • da does not go after an i-adjective. takai da is not correct.

Ii becomes yoi

  • ii (good) cannot be conjugated. Its other form yoi takes over.
  • yokunai means is not good, and yokatta means was good.
  • Never say iikunai or iikatta.

Aru and iru

  • This is an extra that the book does not cover in this chapter.
  • aru (exist) has a special negative, nai. It is not aranai.
  • iru (be present) is Regular, so it is inai, ita and inakatta.

Kuru has three sounds

  • The dictionary form is kuru, and the ta form is kita.
  • The nai form and the nakatta form use ko: konai and konakatta.
  • The masu stem is ki: kimasu, kimashita.

7kutsu o kawanakatta. (くつを かわなかった。)The sentence is negative, so use the nakatta form. First make the nai form, kawanai, and then change the last i to katta.
8daigaku de eigo o oshieta. (だいがくで えいごを おしえた。)The sentence is positive, so use the ta form. Regular verb: drop ru and add ta.
9kinyoubi ni kita. (きんようびに きた。)The sentence is positive, so use the ta form. kuru is Special: the ta form is kita.
10tomodachi to asonda. (ともだちと あそんだ。)The sentence is positive, so use the ta form. asobu ends in bu (Group 1), so bu becomes nda.

Change to negative (page 154)

A present verb becomes the nai form. A past verb becomes the nakatta form.

#AnswerWhy
1hitori de ikanai. (ひとりで いかない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. iku ends in ku, so ku becomes ka and then nai is added.
2raishuu no kayoubi ni yasumanai. (らいしゅうの かようびに やすまない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. yasumu ends in mu, so mu becomes ma and then nai is added.
3minna ni setsumeishinakatta. (みんなに せつめいしなかった。)The sentence is past, so use the nakatta form. First make the nai form, setsumeishinai, and then change the last i to katta.
4hashi de tabenai. (はしで たべない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. Regular verb: drop ru and add nai.
5nihon de hatarakanakatta. (にほんで はたらかなかった。)The sentence is past, so use the nakatta form. First make the nai form, hatarakanai, and then change the last i to katta.
6rainen modoranai. (らいねん もどらない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. modoru ends in ru, so ru becomes ra and then nai is added.
7kippu o kawanakatta. (きっぷを かわなかった。)The sentence is past, so use the nakatta form. First make the nai form, kawanai, and then change the last i to katta.
8me-ru o kakanai. (メールを かかない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. kaku ends in ku, so ku becomes ka and then nai is added.
9densha de ikanakatta. (でんしゃで いかなかった。)The sentence is past, so use the nakatta form. First make the nai form, ikanai, and then change the last i to katta.
10doyoubi ni sentakushinai. (どようびに せんたくしない。)The sentence is present, so use the nai form. sentakusuru is a noun + suru verb, so the nai form ends in shinai.

Choose the correct grammatical pattern (page 157)

Look at the time word and the kind of word that follows. That tells you the tense and the form.

#AnswerWhy
11 tsukuru (つくる)mainichi means every day, which is a habit, so use the dictionary form tsukuru. tsukutta and tsukatta are past, and tsukau means use.
22 tabenai (たべない)amari goes with a negative verb, and maiasa makes it a habit, so use the nai form tabenai. It means I do not eat breakfast much.
34 nonda (のんだ)senshuu means last week, so use the ta form. nomu is Group 1, so mu becomes nda: nonda. nomita, nomuta and nonta are not real forms.
42 kawanai (かわない)The new computer is a little expensive, so I do not buy it now. kau ends in u, so u becomes wa and then nai is added: kawanai. The others are not real forms.
51 okita (おきた)kesa means this morning, so use the ta form. okiru is Regular, so drop ru and add ta: okita. The others are not forms of okiru.
63 dawa (だわ)kirei is a na-adjective, so the soft ending wa needs da in front of it: kirei da wa. A bare wa, nawa and wano do not fit.
74 unten (うんてん)kuruma o unten suru means drive a car. setsumei is an explanation, henji is a reply and kaimono is shopping.
84 matta (まった)B answers in the past (machimashita), so A asks with the ta form. matsu is Group 5, so tsu becomes tta: matta. mata means again.

Rearrange the words (page 158)

Each answer shows the order of the four words and the full sentence.

#AnswerWhy
14 1 3 2: watashi wa mainichi ge-mu o suru. (わたしは まいにち ゲームを する。)I play games every day. The time word comes first, then the thing with o, and the verb is last.
24 3 1 2: ashita no pa-ti- e konai no? (あしたの パーティーへ こないの？)Are you not coming to tomorrow's party? The place comes first, then e, then the nai form, and no at the end makes it a casual question. The book prints a full stop here, but no after a verb marks a question.
34 2 1 3: yamada san wa maishuu kinyoubi ni heya o soujisuru. (やまださんは まいしゅう きんようびに へやを そうじする。)Yamada cleans the room on Fridays every week. A day of the week takes ni, and heya takes o. The verb soujisuru is already printed.
42 1 4 3: kinou no yoru taijin no tomodachi to hanabi o mita. (きのうの よる タイじんの ともだちと はなびを みた。)Last night I watched fireworks with a Thai friend. The time comes first, then taijin no tomodachi to for the companion, then hanabi. The o is printed after the blanks.
53 2 4 1: imouto wa maiasa zenzen hayaku okinai. (いもうとは まいあさ ぜんぜん はやく おきない。)My younger sister never gets up early in the morning. The time word comes first, and zenzen sits right before hayaku and the negative verb okinai. If your key puts hayaku before zenzen, that is only a small difference in word order.
64 1 3 2: otousan wa osake to ko-ra o amari nomanai. (おとうさんは おさけとコーラを あまり のまない。)My father does not drink alcohol and cola much. osake to ko-ra is the thing, o marks it, and amari goes with the negative verb nomanai.
73 1 4 2: watashi wa kinou kouen no mae de matta. (わたしは きのう こうえんの まえで まった。)I waited in front of the park yesterday. kouen no mae means in front of the park, and de marks where the waiting happened.
82 4 1 3: kyonen kim san to nihongo o nihon de benkyoushita. (きょねん キムさんと にほんごを にほんで べんきょうした。)Last year I studied Japanese in Japan with Kim. to marks the companion, nihongo o is what was studied, and nihon de is the place. The de is printed after the blanks.

Fill in the proper word or phrase (page 159)

The passage is a trip to Sapporo last February with the family. It was cold and pretty, and the writer enjoyed the snow festival, a hot spring and skiing.

#AnswerWhy
14 kisetsu (きせつ)fuyu no kisetsu means the winter season. The other choices are a photo, a game and laundry, and none of them fits after fuyu no.
24 gonin (ごにん)The writer went with father, mother, an older sister and an older brother. Counting the writer, that is five people, so gonin de. If you count only the four relatives, you get yonin, but the writer is travelling too.
31 tanoshikatta (たのしかった)The trip happened last year, and the sentence before it is past (deshita), so use the past positive tanoshikatta. totemo tanoshikatta desu means it was very fun.

Read and answer (page 160)

Ana tells Jon that she is well and that it is still a little cold in Japan. She saw the cherry blossoms at a park last Sunday, says she is busy at work, and will fly home to the Philippines on the 15th next month.

#AnswerWhy
11 kouen (こうえん)The letter says senshuu no nichiyoubi ni kaisha no tomodachi to kouen de hanami o mimashita. Ana went to a park to see the cherry blossoms with friends from work.
24 hitori de kaerimasu (ひとりで かえります)The letter only says juugonichi ni firipin e kaerimasu, and it names nobody to go with. Jon is the person she writes to, the friends from work were at the park, and the family trip was Jon's, so the only choice left is hitori de (alone).

Questions and answers in sentence form (page 161)

These ask about you, so the answers below are samples. Each one shows the pattern the question is drilling. Any true answer in a casual sentence works. A negative answer also works, for example iie, shinai.

#AnswerWhy
1kuji kara goji made shigotosuru. (くじから ごじまで しごとする。)nanji kara nanji made asks for a start time and an end time. Choose benkyousuru or shigotosuru. Sample meaning: I work from nine to five.
2hai, mainichi benkyousuru. isshuukan ni gojikan benkyousuru. (はい、まいにち べんきょうする。いっしゅうかんに ごじかん べんきょうする。)The first question is a yes or no question, so start with hai or iie. nanjikan asks how many hours. Sample meaning: Yes, I study every day. I study five hours a week.
3ichinichi ni sanjikan gurai keitai o tsukau. (いちにちに さんじかんぐらい けいたいを つかう。)dono gurai asks how long. Answer with an amount of time and tsukau. Sample meaning: I use my cell phone for about three hours a day.
4hai, taberu. resutoran de taberu. (はい、たべる。レストランで たべる。)The first question is yes or no. doko de asks where, so answer with a place and de. Sample meaning: Yes, I do. I eat at a restaurant.
5hai, suru. tenisusuru. (はい、する。テニスする。)nan no supo-tsu asks which sport. A sport takes suru, so tenisusuru. Sample meaning: Yes, I do. I play tennis.
6hai, mita. nihon no eiga o mita. (はい、みた。にほんの えいがを みた。)The question is in the past, so use mita. nani o asks what. Sample meaning: Yes, I did. I watched a Japanese movie.
7hai, maishuu soujisuru. (はい、まいしゅう そうじする。)This is a yes or no question about a habit, so answer with hai or iie and the dictionary form. Sample meaning: Yes, I clean every week.
8kazoku to nihon e iku. (かぞくと にほんへ いく。)doko asks where, so name a place. The marker e is kept here, and it can also be dropped. Sample meaning: I will go to Japan with my family.
9hai, itta. mo-ru de kaimonoshita. (はい、いった。モールで かいものした。)The first question is past and yes or no, so answer with itta. nani o asks what you did. Sample meaning: Yes, I went. I went shopping at the mall.
10kouen e iku. (こうえんへ いく。)doko e asks where to, so answer with a place and e. Sample meaning: I will go to the park.

Translate into Japanese (page 161)

These answers are casual, to match the chapter. The formal masu style is also correct. Word order can shift a little in all of them, as long as the verb stays last.

#AnswerWhy
1konban tomodachi to dekakeru. (こんばん ともだちと でかける。)dekakeru means go out. It is a Regular verb, and the dictionary form covers the future. to marks the companion, and konban takes no ni.
2ashita sensei ni soudansuru. (あした せんせいに そうだんする。)soudansuru takes ni for the person you consult. ashita takes no ni.
3kurasume-to ni setsumeisuru. (クラスメートに せつめいする。)setsumeisuru takes ni for the person you explain to. kurasume-to is a classmate, with a hyphen for the long vowel.
4mainichi gakkou de renshuusuru. (まいにち がっこうで れんしゅうする。)de marks the place of the action. mainichi takes no ni. renshuusuru means practice.
5kinou rokujikan kuruma o untenshita. (きのう ろくじかん くるまを うんてんした。)kuruma o untensuru means drive a car, and the past is untenshita. rokujikan is a length of time, and it takes no particle.
6konshuu no nichiyoubi ni tomodachi to gorufusuru. (こんしゅうの にちようびに ともだちと ゴルフする。)ni marks the day of the week. A sport takes suru, so golf is gorufusuru.
7isshuukan ni ichido heya o soujisuru. (いっしゅうかんに いちど へやを そうじする。)isshuukan ni ichido means once a week. heya o soujisuru is clean the room.
8maishuu getsuyoubi ni joushi ni repo-to o dasu. (まいしゅう げつようびに じょうしに レポートを だす。)joushi is a supervisor, and ni marks the person you hand the report to. dasu means submit.
9tenisu wa shinai. / tenisushinai. (テニスは しない。 / テニスしない。)A sport takes suru, so the negative is shinai. In a negative sentence o can change to wa for emphasis, and tenisushinai also works.
10konban hitori de hanabi o miru. (こんばん ひとりで はなびを みる。)hitori de means alone. hanabi o miru is watch fireworks, and the dictionary form covers the future.
